Ok @hvaara thanks for your patience! Here's the results from my deep dive to the traces of metal resources getting generated during the execution of the code snippet and my current understanding on what's going on:

    The memory grows by the size of the output object of linear layer for each iteration run so by 4 * N * C * H * W bytes, making sense since this is the output object we allocate on L50 in the linear op 1
    When the executeMPSGraph is called using COMMIT_ADAPTIVE as the SyncMode, the operation is encoded to the active command buffer in MPSStream but unless the memory pressure is too high, the command buffer is not committed but instead we keep on encoding operations to the same command buffer 2
    Since each iteration with the nn.Linear needs to maintain its own output tensor until the computation is completed and the python object goes out of scope to be garbage collected, we see the memory increase while the command buffer keeps accumulating more encoded operations. In case we change to COMMIT_AND_WAIT as our SyncMode the command buffers get committed after each encode and the memory buffers required for the outputs are also released once the computation returns. This probably lets the garbage collector sees that the object is no longer needed since we don't assign the outputs of the computation to anything in the python script.
    To validate this I tried to adjust the original script slightly to allow for the adaptive commit to run its course and the computations to return so that the underlying objects can be released and we can see the memory get freed up. It seems like on my local setup it takes about 5-6s of waiting for the objects to get cleaned up. In actual code I assume this would happen more often since there can be other operations calling the command buffer to get synchronized in between in order to perform updates based on the results.

So in summary to me it seems like the memory is managed as intended in this case. In its current form the COMMIT_ADAPTIVE is a bit opaque to the user since it might make the memory seem like its behaving erratically as the commit is automated to only happen once the local device hits the low memory watermark, which depends on the device you are running on. Additionally there's the interplay of when will the underlying python objects get garbage collected that should finally release the memory buffers assigned to them. Let me know if this sounds reasonable or if you think there's still something we missed here. Or if this is causing a concrete issue on your side that would warrant us to do some changes on how the adaptive commit works at the moment.
rephrased_statement: Observed memory increase of 4 × N × C × H × W bytes per iteration, matching the allocation size of the linear layer output object.

original_statement:
Let me give you some background on this issue from the NCCL team's perspective:
 Until recently, ncclCommGetAsyncError was, as @ptrblck said, a pure read-op. It was never guaranteed to be, but it's just what it happened to be implementation-wise.
 This changed in NCCL 2.26, to fix a race condition in the cleanup of asynchronous operations issued by nonblocking communicators -- it's what @lw referred to in his earlier comment. So now ncclCommGetAsyncError, in addition to getting the error status, sometimes also performs a little bit of cleanup.
rephrased_statement: To provide some background from the NCCL team, ncclCommGetAsyncError used to act as a simple read‑only query; although the API never formally declared it read‑only, the implementation up to version 2.25 performed no mutation. In NCCL 2.26 we altered this behavior to fix a race condition that could occur during the teardown of asynchronous operations issued by non‑blocking communicators. The fix injects a lightweight cleanup routine into ncclCommGetAsyncError, so the call now both reports the error status and, when necessary, clears residual asynchronous state. This dual purpose resolves the race but also changes the contract of the function, meaning it is no longer guaranteed to be a pure read operation.

original_statement: torch.export.export() uses fake tensors during graph tracing, which don't have actual memory storage. The RNN module's flatten_parameters() method was calling p.data_ptr() for aliasing detection, causing "Cannot access data pointer of Tensor" errors on GPU.
rephrased_statement: The export utility torch.export.export() works by tracing the model using fake tensors—objects that carry shape, dtype, and device information but do not allocate buffer space. Inside the RNN implementation, flatten_parameters() calls p.data_ptr() to see if parameters share the same underlying buffer (aliasing). Since the fake tensors used during tracing have no underlying buffer, the data_ptr() request cannot be satisfied, and PyTorch raises a “Cannot access data pointer of Tensor” error when the export is performed on a GPU.

  File "/Users/miccoli/work/uvenv/bigdata/.venv/lib/python3.12/site-packages/numpy/_core/fromnumeric.py", line 3858, in mean
    return mean(axis=axis, dtype=dtype, out=out, **kwargs)

original_statement:
Ok @hvaara thanks for your patience! Here's the results from my deep dive to the traces of metal resources getting generated during the execution of the code snippet and my current understanding on what's going on:

    The memory grows by the size of the output object of linear layer for each iteration run so by 4 * N * C * H * W bytes, making sense since this is the output object we allocate on L50 in the linear op 1
    When the executeMPSGraph is called using COMMIT_ADAPTIVE as the SyncMode, the operation is encoded to the active command buffer in MPSStream but unless the memory pressure is too high, the command buffer is not committed but instead we keep on encoding operations to the same command buffer 2
    Since each iteration with the nn.Linear needs to maintain its own output tensor until the computation is completed and the python object goes out of scope to be garbage collected, we see the memory increase while the command buffer keeps accumulating more encoded operations. In case we change to COMMIT_AND_WAIT as our SyncMode the command buffers get committed after each encode and the memory buffers required for the outputs are also released once the computation returns. This probably lets the garbage collector sees that the object is no longer needed since we don't assign the outputs of the computation to anything in the python script.
    To validate this I tried to adjust the original script slightly to allow for the adaptive commit to run its course and the computations to return so that the underlying objects can be released and we can see the memory get freed up. It seems like on my local setup it takes about 5-6s of waiting for the objects to get cleaned up. In actual code I assume this would happen more often since there can be other operations calling the command buffer to get synchronized in between in order to perform updates based on the results.

So in summary to me it seems like the memory is managed as intended in this case. In its current form the COMMIT_ADAPTIVE is a bit opaque to the user since it might make the memory seem like its behaving erratically as the commit is automated to only happen once the local device hits the low memory watermark, which depends on the device you are running on. Additionally there's the interplay of when will the underlying python objects get garbage collected that should finally release the memory buffers assigned to them. Let me know if this sounds reasonable or if you think there's still something we missed here. Or if this is causing a concrete issue on your side that would warrant us to do some changes on how the adaptive commit works at the moment.
rephrased_statement: Thanks for the patience, @hvaara – after a deep dive into the metal‑resource trace, my current hypothesis is that each iteration inflates the resident set by roughly 4 × N × C × H × W bytes, which matches the size of the Linear layer's output allocated at L50. When MPSGraph is invoked with `SyncMode::COMMIT_ADAPTIVE`, the kernel is enqueued into the active MPSStream command buffer but, unless the device memory pressure crosses the low‑watermark threshold, the buffer remains uncommitted and subsequent ops keep piling onto the same buffer. Because each `nn.Linear` call retains its output tensor until the Python reference is dropped, the memory footprint climbs while the command buffer accumulates work. Switching to `COMMIT_AND_WAIT` forces a buffer flush after every encode, allowing the runtime to release the output buffers once the call returns – this likely gives the GC a chance to reclaim the Python objects, since we never stash the results. I verified this by instrumenting the script to let the adaptive commit run to completion and then sleeping ~5‑6 s, after which the memory usage drops. In practice, on a larger workload the garbage collector would intervene more frequently as other ops synchronize the command buffer. So, to the best of my understanding, the observed growth is expected behavior; the opacity of `COMMIT_ADAPTIVE` stems from its device‑dependent commit policy and the timing of Python‑level deallocation. Let me know if this interpretation aligns with your observations or if there are edge cases we should still address.

Let me give you some background on this issue from the NCCL team's perspective:
 Until recently, ncclCommGetAsyncError was, as @ptrblck said, a pure read-op. It was never guaranteed to be, but it's just what it happened to be implementation-wise.
 This changed in NCCL 2.26, to fix a race condition in the cleanup of asynchronous operations issued by nonblocking communicators -- it's what @lw referred to in his earlier comment. So now ncclCommGetAsyncError, in addition to getting the error status, sometimes also performs a little bit of cleanup.
rephrased_statement: Quick background: ncclCommGetAsyncError’s behavior shifted in NCCL 2.26 to include cleanup steps as part of fixing async operation race issues.

Ok @hvaara thanks for your patience! Here's the results from my deep dive to the traces of metal resources getting generated during the execution of the code snippet and my current understanding on what's going on:

    The memory grows by the size of the output object of linear layer for each iteration run so by 4 * N * C * H * W bytes, making sense since this is the output object we allocate on L50 in the linear op 1
    When the executeMPSGraph is called using COMMIT_ADAPTIVE as the SyncMode, the operation is encoded to the active command buffer in MPSStream but unless the memory pressure is too high, the command buffer is not committed but instead we keep on encoding operations to the same command buffer 2
    Since each iteration with the nn.Linear needs to maintain its own output tensor until the computation is completed and the python object goes out of scope to be garbage collected, we see the memory increase while the command buffer keeps accumulating more encoded operations. In case we change to COMMIT_AND_WAIT as our SyncMode the command buffers get committed after each encode and the memory buffers required for the outputs are also released once the computation returns. This probably lets the garbage collector sees that the object is no longer needed since we don't assign the outputs of the computation to anything in the python script.
    To validate this I tried to adjust the original script slightly to allow for the adaptive commit to run its course and the computations to return so that the underlying objects can be released and we can see the memory get freed up. It seems like on my local setup it takes about 5-6s of waiting for the objects to get cleaned up. In actual code I assume this would happen more often since there can be other operations calling the command buffer to get synchronized in between in order to perform updates based on the results.

So in summary to me it seems like the memory is managed as intended in this case. In its current form the COMMIT_ADAPTIVE is a bit opaque to the user since it might make the memory seem like its behaving erratically as the commit is automated to only happen once the local device hits the low memory watermark, which depends on the device you are running on. Additionally there's the interplay of when will the underlying python objects get garbage collected that should finally release the memory buffers assigned to them. Let me know if this sounds reasonable or if you think there's still something we missed here. Or if this is causing a concrete issue on your side that would warrant us to do some changes on how the adaptive commit works at the moment.
rephrased_statement: Calling executeMPSGraph with SyncMode COMMIT_ADAPTIVE encodes operations to the active MPSStream command buffer without immediate commitment unless memory pressure exceeds a threshold.

original_statement: It turns out this was a difference in inflate/deflate implementations between the extension/SDK and the CLI. The SDK uses Node's zlib bindings, while by default Rust's flate2 library uses a rust port of miniz. miniz does not appear to flush decompressed data as nicely on SYNC'd boundaries as zlib does, which caused data to 'stall'. This could also be the cause of some connection flakiness!
rephrased_statement: The discrepancy we were seeing stemmed from the fact that the SDK and the CLI were not using the same compression backend. In the SDK we call into Node's `zlib` module, which implements the standard inflate/deflate algorithm with proper handling of SYNC points. By contrast, the CLI ships with Rust's `flate2` crate, which by default wraps a Rust‑ported version of `miniz`. Unlike zlib, `miniz` tends to leave some decompressed bytes buffered when it encounters a SYNC marker, so the data appears to "stall" until the buffer is eventually flushed. This behavior not only explains the observed latency but also provides a plausible explanation for the occasional connection drops we have been experiencing.

This issue is motivated by ongoing work in SciPy to improve the existing multivariate distributions and add new ones. We'd like to be sure that, if possible, enhancements that we make remain consistent with the current and future behavior of NumPy's multivariate distributions.

The specific issue is how the size parameter interacts with broadcasting of the distribution parameters, some of which are 1-d or 2-d arrays rather than scalars.

I'm going to refer to gufunc broadcasting, so it will be helpful to have the gufunc signatures of the existing multivariate distributions (even though they are not actually implemented as gufuncs):

Name                         Parameters      Gufunc signature
---------------------------  --------------  ----------------
dirichlet                    alpha           (n)       -> (n)
multinomial                  n, pvals        (),(n)    -> (n)
multivariate_normal          mean, cov       (n),(n,n) -> (n)
multivariate_hypergeometric  colors, nsample (n),()    -> (n)

@bashtage has a pull request to add broadcasting to multinomial. As an example, suppose I have four values of n, say 2, 5, 10 and 20, and I have two discrete probability distributions of length 3, say [0.1, 0.2, 0.7] and [0.8, 0.2, 0.0], and I want to generate 10 multinomial variates for each combination of those inputs. With the code in @bashtage's PR, we can write:

In [85]: n = np.array([2, 5, 10, 20]).reshape(-1, 1)

In [86]: pvals = np.array([[0.1, 0.2, 0.7], [0.8, 0.2, 0.0]])

In [87]: rng = np.random.default_rng()

In [88]: x = rng.multinomial(n, pvals, size=(10, 4, 2))

In [89]: x.shape
Out[89]: (10, 4, 2, 3)

The shape of the output has three sources: (10,) is the number of variates that we wanted for each combination of input parameters; (4, 2) is the broadcast shape of the input parameters, without the dimension associated with the gufunc signature; (3,) is the dimension associated with each variate.

Note that size is not the shape of the output array--size does not include the dimension associated with the variates themselves.

The question is how to adapt this to the other multivariate distribution methods.
rephrased_statement: A pull request by @bashtage introduces broadcasting support for `multinomial`, demonstrated with example arrays for `n` and `pvals` and a call to `rng.multinomial` with a specified `size`.

Let me give you some background on this issue from the NCCL team's perspective:
 Until recently, ncclCommGetAsyncError was, as @ptrblck said, a pure read-op. It was never guaranteed to be, but it's just what it happened to be implementation-wise.
 This changed in NCCL 2.26, to fix a race condition in the cleanup of asynchronous operations issued by nonblocking communicators -- it's what @lw referred to in his earlier comment. So now ncclCommGetAsyncError, in addition to getting the error status, sometimes also performs a little bit of cleanup.
rephrased_statement: ncclCommGetAsyncError was originally a pure read‑only call, but since NCCL 2.26 it also performs cleanup to resolve a race condition in non‑blocking communicator shutdowns.

This issue is motivated by ongoing work in SciPy to improve the existing multivariate distributions and add new ones. We'd like to be sure that, if possible, enhancements that we make remain consistent with the current and future behavior of NumPy's multivariate distributions.

The specific issue is how the size parameter interacts with broadcasting of the distribution parameters, some of which are 1-d or 2-d arrays rather than scalars.

I'm going to refer to gufunc broadcasting, so it will be helpful to have the gufunc signatures of the existing multivariate distributions (even though they are not actually implemented as gufuncs):

Name                         Parameters      Gufunc signature
---------------------------  --------------  ----------------
dirichlet                    alpha           (n)       -> (n)
multinomial                  n, pvals        (),(n)    -> (n)
multivariate_normal          mean, cov       (n),(n,n) -> (n)
multivariate_hypergeometric  colors, nsample (n),()    -> (n)

@bashtage has a pull request to add broadcasting to multinomial. As an example, suppose I have four values of n, say 2, 5, 10 and 20, and I have two discrete probability distributions of length 3, say [0.1, 0.2, 0.7] and [0.8, 0.2, 0.0], and I want to generate 10 multinomial variates for each combination of those inputs. With the code in @bashtage's PR, we can write:

In [85]: n = np.array([2, 5, 10, 20]).reshape(-1, 1)

In [86]: pvals = np.array([[0.1, 0.2, 0.7], [0.8, 0.2, 0.0]])

In [87]: rng = np.random.default_rng()

In [88]: x = rng.multinomial(n, pvals, size=(10, 4, 2))

In [89]: x.shape
Out[89]: (10, 4, 2, 3)

The shape of the output has three sources: (10,) is the number of variates that we wanted for each combination of input parameters; (4, 2) is the broadcast shape of the input parameters, without the dimension associated with the gufunc signature; (3,) is the dimension associated with each variate.

Note that size is not the shape of the output array--size does not include the dimension associated with the variates themselves.

The question is how to adapt this to the other multivariate distribution methods.
rephrased_statement: Including the example from @bashtage's PR that demonstrates broadcasting with `rng.multinomial` and the resulting output shape.

Let me give you some background on this issue from the NCCL team's perspective:
 Until recently, ncclCommGetAsyncError was, as @ptrblck said, a pure read-op. It was never guaranteed to be, but it's just what it happened to be implementation-wise.
 This changed in NCCL 2.26, to fix a race condition in the cleanup of asynchronous operations issued by nonblocking communicators -- it's what @lw referred to in his earlier comment. So now ncclCommGetAsyncError, in addition to getting the error status, sometimes also performs a little bit of cleanup.

Ok @hvaara thanks for your patience! Here's the results from my deep dive to the traces of metal resources getting generated during the execution of the code snippet and my current understanding on what's going on:

    The memory grows by the size of the output object of linear layer for each iteration run so by 4 * N * C * H * W bytes, making sense since this is the output object we allocate on L50 in the linear op 1
    When the executeMPSGraph is called using COMMIT_ADAPTIVE as the SyncMode, the operation is encoded to the active command buffer in MPSStream but unless the memory pressure is too high, the command buffer is not committed but instead we keep on encoding operations to the same command buffer 2
    Since each iteration with the nn.Linear needs to maintain its own output tensor until the computation is completed and the python object goes out of scope to be garbage collected, we see the memory increase while the command buffer keeps accumulating more encoded operations. In case we change to COMMIT_AND_WAIT as our SyncMode the command buffers get committed after each encode and the memory buffers required for the outputs are also released once the computation returns. This probably lets the garbage collector sees that the object is no longer needed since we don't assign the outputs of the computation to anything in the python script.
    To validate this I tried to adjust the original script slightly to allow for the adaptive commit to run its course and the computations to return so that the underlying objects can be released and we can see the memory get freed up. It seems like on my local setup it takes about 5-6s of waiting for the objects to get cleaned up. In actual code I assume this would happen more often since there can be other operations calling the command buffer to get synchronized in between in order to perform updates based on the results.

So in summary to me it seems like the memory is managed as intended in this case. In its current form the COMMIT_ADAPTIVE is a bit opaque to the user since it might make the memory seem like its behaving erratically as the commit is automated to only happen once the local device hits the low memory watermark, which depends on the device you are running on. Additionally there's the interplay of when will the underlying python objects get garbage collected that should finally release the memory buffers assigned to them. Let me know if this sounds reasonable or if you think there's still something we missed here. Or if this is causing a concrete issue on your side that would warrant us to do some changes on how the adaptive commit works at the moment.
rephrased_statement: After a deep dive into the metal resource traces, here’s what I’ve uncovered: each iteration allocates an output tensor for the linear layer, consuming 4 × N × C × H × W bytes—this explains the steady memory growth we observe at L50. With the SyncMode set to COMMIT_ADAPTIVE, MPSStream keeps encoding operations into a single command buffer, postponing the actual commit until the GPU’s memory pressure reaches a low‑watermark. Consequently, the output tensors remain alive until the Python objects fall out of scope and the garbage collector finally frees them. If we change the SyncMode to COMMIT_AND_WAIT, the command buffer is committed after every encode, and the associated memory buffers are released immediately after the computation returns, which also helps the GC recognize that the objects are no longer needed. In my experiments, I had to wait about 5‑6 seconds for the cleanup to occur on my machine, but in a real application the timing will depend on how often other operations synchronize the command buffer. Overall, the observed memory pattern aligns with the intended behavior of the adaptive commit mechanism; it just hides the commit points behind device‑specific thresholds, making the memory usage appear sporadic.

This issue is motivated by ongoing work in SciPy to improve the existing multivariate distributions and add new ones. We'd like to be sure that, if possible, enhancements that we make remain consistent with the current and future behavior of NumPy's multivariate distributions.

The specific issue is how the size parameter interacts with broadcasting of the distribution parameters, some of which are 1-d or 2-d arrays rather than scalars.

I'm going to refer to gufunc broadcasting, so it will be helpful to have the gufunc signatures of the existing multivariate distributions (even though they are not actually implemented as gufuncs):

Name                         Parameters      Gufunc signature
---------------------------  --------------  ----------------
dirichlet                    alpha           (n)       -> (n)
multinomial                  n, pvals        (),(n)    -> (n)
multivariate_normal          mean, cov       (n),(n,n) -> (n)
multivariate_hypergeometric  colors, nsample (n),()    -> (n)

@bashtage has a pull request to add broadcasting to multinomial. As an example, suppose I have four values of n, say 2, 5, 10 and 20, and I have two discrete probability distributions of length 3, say [0.1, 0.2, 0.7] and [0.8, 0.2, 0.0], and I want to generate 10 multinomial variates for each combination of those inputs. With the code in @bashtage's PR, we can write:

In [85]: n = np.array([2, 5, 10, 20]).reshape(-1, 1)

In [86]: pvals = np.array([[0.1, 0.2, 0.7], [0.8, 0.2, 0.0]])

In [87]: rng = np.random.default_rng()

In [88]: x = rng.multinomial(n, pvals, size=(10, 4, 2))

In [89]: x.shape
Out[89]: (10, 4, 2, 3)

The shape of the output has three sources: (10,) is the number of variates that we wanted for each combination of input parameters; (4, 2) is the broadcast shape of the input parameters, without the dimension associated with the gufunc signature; (3,) is the dimension associated with each variate.

Note that size is not the shape of the output array--size does not include the dimension associated with the variates themselves.

The question is how to adapt this to the other multivariate distribution methods.
rephrased_statement: Opening a discussion on adapting the broadcasting approach used for Multinomial to other multivariate distribution methods.

Using MPS for BERT inference appears to produce about a 2x slowdown compared to the CPU. Here is code to reproduce the issue:
 # MPS Version
 from transformers import AutoTokenizer, BertForSequenceClassification
 import timeit
 import torch
 

 tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained("bert-base-cased")
 model = BertForSequenceClassification.from_pretrained("bert-base-cased").to(torch.device("mps"))
 

 tokens = tokenizer.tokenize("Hello world, this is michael!")
 tids = tokenizer.convert_tokens_to_ids(tokens)
 with torch.no_grad():
  t_tids = torch.tensor([tids]*64, device=torch.device("mps"))
  res = timeit.timeit(lambda: model(input_ids=t_tids), number=100)
 print(res)
 

 torch.backends.mps.is_available() reports True as expected.
 I chose a batch size of 64, since that was mentioned on the blog post for the ~5x speedup in Huggingface BERT.
 Running this benchmark, swapping "mps" and "cpu" for the devices, I get:
 CPU 18.38 s
 MPS 36.00 s

 CUDA 0.82 s
 I used the no_grad() construction due to the comment mentioned on #77753.
 I used today's nightly build. Furthermore, I also built PyTorch from source and observed no differences on the results here. Previously, NpyIter_GetIterNext was declared as returning a pointer (NpyIter_IterNextFunc*), which contradicts the actual C prototype that yields a function object (NpyIter_IterNextFunc). The correction aligns the Cython cdef with the true C definition, thereby preventing the "incompatible function pointer" errors that arise when users compile Cython code that invokes this iterator helper. After the change, the generated C code matches the expected signature and the build process completes cleanly across all supported platforms.

Let me give you some background on this issue from the NCCL team's perspective:
 Until recently, ncclCommGetAsyncError was, as @ptrblck said, a pure read-op. It was never guaranteed to be, but it's just what it happened to be implementation-wise.
 This changed in NCCL 2.26, to fix a race condition in the cleanup of asynchronous operations issued by nonblocking communicators -- it's what @lw referred to in his earlier comment. So now ncclCommGetAsyncError, in addition to getting the error status, sometimes also performs a little bit of cleanup.

Ok @hvaara thanks for your patience! Here's the results from my deep dive to the traces of metal resources getting generated during the execution of the code snippet and my current understanding on what's going on:

    The memory grows by the size of the output object of linear layer for each iteration run so by 4 * N * C * H * W bytes, making sense since this is the output object we allocate on L50 in the linear op 1
    When the executeMPSGraph is called using COMMIT_ADAPTIVE as the SyncMode, the operation is encoded to the active command buffer in MPSStream but unless the memory pressure is too high, the command buffer is not committed but instead we keep on encoding operations to the same command buffer 2
    Since each iteration with the nn.Linear needs to maintain its own output tensor until the computation is completed and the python object goes out of scope to be garbage collected, we see the memory increase while the command buffer keeps accumulating more encoded operations. In case we change to COMMIT_AND_WAIT as our SyncMode the command buffers get committed after each encode and the memory buffers required for the outputs are also released once the computation returns. This probably lets the garbage collector sees that the object is no longer needed since we don't assign the outputs of the computation to anything in the python script.
    To validate this I tried to adjust the original script slightly to allow for the adaptive commit to run its course and the computations to return so that the underlying objects can be released and we can see the memory get freed up. This issue is motivated by ongoing work in SciPy to improve the existing multivariate distributions and add new ones. We'd like to be sure that, if possible, enhancements that we make remain consistent with the current and future behavior of NumPy's multivariate distributions.

The specific issue is how the size parameter interacts with broadcasting of the distribution parameters, some of which are 1-d or 2-d arrays rather than scalars.

I'm going to refer to gufunc broadcasting, so it will be helpful to have the gufunc signatures of the existing multivariate distributions (even though they are not actually implemented as gufuncs):

Name                         Parameters      Gufunc signature
---------------------------  --------------  ----------------
dirichlet                    alpha           (n)       -> (n)
multinomial                  n, pvals        (),(n)    -> (n)
multivariate_normal          mean, cov       (n),(n,n) -> (n)
multivariate_hypergeometric  colors, nsample (n),()    -> (n)

@bashtage has a pull request to add broadcasting to multinomial. As an example, suppose I have four values of n, say 2, 5, 10 and 20, and I have two discrete probability distributions of length 3, say [0.1, 0.2, 0.7] and [0.8, 0.2, 0.0], and I want to generate 10 multinomial variates for each combination of those inputs. With the code in @bashtage's PR, we can write:

In [85]: n = np.array([2, 5, 10, 20]).reshape(-1, 1)

In [86]: pvals = np.array([[0.1, 0.2, 0.7], [0.8, 0.2, 0.0]])

In [87]: rng = np.random.default_rng()

In [88]: x = rng.multinomial(n, pvals, size=(10, 4, 2))

In [89]: x.shape
Out[89]: (10, 4, 2, 3)

The shape of the output has three sources: (10,) is the number of variates that we wanted for each combination of input parameters; (4, 2) is the broadcast shape of the input parameters, without the dimension associated with the gufunc signature; (3,) is the dimension associated with each variate.

Note that size is not the shape of the output array--size does not include the dimension associated with the variates themselves.

The question is how to adapt this to the other multivariate distribution methods.
rephrased_statement: SciPy development includes updates to existing multivariate distributions and addition of new ones, with a goal of maintaining consistency with NumPy's multivariate distribution behavior.

This issue is motivated by ongoing work in SciPy to improve the existing multivariate distributions and add new ones. We'd like to be sure that, if possible, enhancements that we make remain consistent with the current and future behavior of NumPy's multivariate distributions.

The specific issue is how the size parameter interacts with broadcasting of the distribution parameters, some of which are 1-d or 2-d arrays rather than scalars.

I'm going to refer to gufunc broadcasting, so it will be helpful to have the gufunc signatures of the existing multivariate distributions (even though they are not actually implemented as gufuncs):

Name                         Parameters      Gufunc signature
---------------------------  --------------  ----------------
dirichlet                    alpha           (n)       -> (n)
multinomial                  n, pvals        (),(n)    -> (n)
multivariate_normal          mean, cov       (n),(n,n) -> (n)
multivariate_hypergeometric  colors, nsample (n),()    -> (n)

@bashtage has a pull request to add broadcasting to multinomial. As an example, suppose I have four values of n, say 2, 5, 10 and 20, and I have two discrete probability distributions of length 3, say [0.1, 0.2, 0.7] and [0.8, 0.2, 0.0], and I want to generate 10 multinomial variates for each combination of those inputs. With the code in @bashtage's PR, we can write:

In [85]: n = np.array([2, 5, 10, 20]).reshape(-1, 1)

In [86]: pvals = np.array([[0.1, 0.2, 0.7], [0.8, 0.2, 0.0]])

In [87]: rng = np.random.default_rng()

In [88]: x = rng.multinomial(n, pvals, size=(10, 4, 2))

In [89]: x.shape
Out[89]: (10, 4, 2, 3)

The shape of the output has three sources: (10,) is the number of variates that we wanted for each combination of input parameters; (4, 2) is the broadcast shape of the input parameters, without the dimension associated with the gufunc signature; (3,) is the dimension associated with each variate.

Note that size is not the shape of the output array--size does not include the dimension associated with the variates themselves.

The question is how to adapt this to the other multivariate distribution methods.
rephrased_statement: Reference gufunc signatures for existing multivariate distributions (e.g., dirichlet: (n)->(n), multinomial: (),(n)->(n), multivariate_normal: (n),(n,n)->(n), multivariate_hypergeometric: (n),()->(n)) are listed for context.

original_statement: torch.export.export() uses fake tensors during graph tracing, which don't have actual memory storage. The RNN module's flatten_parameters() method was calling p.data_ptr() for aliasing detection, causing "Cannot access data pointer of Tensor" errors on GPU.
rephrased_statement: While exporting a model with torch.export.export(), PyTorch creates placeholder tensors (fake tensors) that mimic the original tensors’ metadata but omit any actual memory allocation. The RNN module’s flatten_parameters() function still attempts to obtain the raw memory address of its weight tensors via the data_ptr() method for the purpose of consolidating parameter storage. Because fake tensors do not have a real address, this call crashes on CUDA, producing the “Cannot access data pointer of Tensor” message.

original_statement:
Ok @hvaara thanks for your patience! Here's the results from my deep dive to the traces of metal resources getting generated during the execution of the code snippet and my current understanding on what's going on:

    The memory grows by the size of the output object of linear layer for each iteration run so by 4 * N * C * H * W bytes, making sense since this is the output object we allocate on L50 in the linear op 1
    When the executeMPSGraph is called using COMMIT_ADAPTIVE as the SyncMode, the operation is encoded to the active command buffer in MPSStream but unless the memory pressure is too high, the command buffer is not committed but instead we keep on encoding operations to the same command buffer 2
    Since each iteration with the nn.Linear needs to maintain its own output tensor until the computation is completed and the python object goes out of scope to be garbage collected, we see the memory increase while the command buffer keeps accumulating more encoded operations. In case we change to COMMIT_AND_WAIT as our SyncMode the command buffers get committed after each encode and the memory buffers required for the outputs are also released once the computation returns. This probably lets the garbage collector sees that the object is no longer needed since we don't assign the outputs of the computation to anything in the python script.
    To validate this I tried to adjust the original script slightly to allow for the adaptive commit to run its course and the computations to return so that the underlying objects can be released and we can see the memory get freed up. It seems like on my local setup it takes about 5-6s of waiting for the objects to get cleaned up. In actual code I assume this would happen more often since there can be other operations calling the command buffer to get synchronized in between in order to perform updates based on the results.

So in summary to me it seems like the memory is managed as intended in this case. In its current form the COMMIT_ADAPTIVE is a bit opaque to the user since it might make the memory seem like its behaving erratically as the commit is automated to only happen once the local device hits the low memory watermark, which depends on the device you are running on. Additionally there's the interplay of when will the underlying python objects get garbage collected that should finally release the memory buffers assigned to them. Let me know if this sounds reasonable or if you think there's still something we missed here. Or if this is causing a concrete issue on your side that would warrant us to do some changes on how the adaptive commit works at the moment.
rephrased_statement: I appreciate your patience, @hvaara – the trace analysis indicates that each loop iteration allocates roughly 4 × N × C × H × W bytes, which aligns with the Linear layer's output created at line 50. With `SyncMode::COMMIT_ADAPTIVE`, `executeMPSGraph` enqueues the kernel into the current MPSStream command buffer but postpones the commit until memory pressure reaches a threshold, so the same buffer keeps absorbing new commands. Because the `nn.Linear` output tensors remain referenced in Python until they go out of scope, the process's memory footprint grows while the command buffer accumulates work. If we opt for `COMMIT_AND_WAIT`, each encode triggers an immediate buffer commit, allowing the output buffers to be released once the call returns – this likely enables the garbage collector to reclaim the tensors, as we never store the results. I tested this by permitting the adaptive commit to finish and then inserting a ~5‑6 second delay, after which the memory usage decreased. In a full application, other synchronization points would cause similar GC activity. Hence, my working theory is that the memory behavior is intentional; `COMMIT_ADAPTIVE` appears opaque because its commit timing is contingent on the device's low‑memory watermark and the lifecycle of the Python objects. Please let me know if this matches your findings or if further tweaks are required.

Let me give you some background on this issue from the NCCL team's perspective:
 Until recently, ncclCommGetAsyncError was, as @ptrblck said, a pure read-op. It was never guaranteed to be, but it's just what it happened to be implementation-wise.
 This changed in NCCL 2.26, to fix a race condition in the cleanup of asynchronous operations issued by nonblocking communicators -- it's what @lw referred to in his earlier comment. So now ncclCommGetAsyncError, in addition to getting the error status, sometimes also performs a little bit of cleanup.

Ok @hvaara thanks for your patience! Here's the results from my deep dive to the traces of metal resources getting generated during the execution of the code snippet and my current understanding on what's going on:

    The memory grows by the size of the output object of linear layer for each iteration run so by 4 * N * C * H * W bytes, making sense since this is the output object we allocate on L50 in the linear op 1
    When the executeMPSGraph is called using COMMIT_ADAPTIVE as the SyncMode, the operation is encoded to the active command buffer in MPSStream but unless the memory pressure is too high, the command buffer is not committed but instead we keep on encoding operations to the same command buffer 2
    Since each iteration with the nn.Linear needs to maintain its own output tensor until the computation is completed and the python object goes out of scope to be garbage collected, we see the memory increase while the command buffer keeps accumulating more encoded operations. In case we change to COMMIT_AND_WAIT as our SyncMode the command buffers get committed after each encode and the memory buffers required for the outputs are also released once the computation returns. This probably lets the garbage collector sees that the object is no longer needed since we don't assign the outputs of the computation to anything in the python script.
    To validate this I tried to adjust the original script slightly to allow for the adaptive commit to run its course and the computations to return so that the underlying objects can be released and we can see the memory get freed up. It seems like on my local setup it takes about 5-6s of waiting for the objects to get cleaned up. In actual code I assume this would happen more often since there can be other operations calling the command buffer to get synchronized in between in order to perform updates based on the results.

So in summary to me it seems like the memory is managed as intended in this case. In its current form the COMMIT_ADAPTIVE is a bit opaque to the user since it might make the memory seem like its behaving erratically as the commit is automated to only happen once the local device hits the low memory watermark, which depends on the device you are running on. Additionally there's the interplay of when will the underlying python objects get garbage collected that should finally release the memory buffers assigned to them. Let me know if this sounds reasonable or if you think there's still something we missed here. Or if this is causing a concrete issue on your side that would warrant us to do some changes on how the adaptive commit works at the moment.
rephrased_statement: Thanks for waiting, @hvaara! Quick rundown: every loop adds an output tensor from the linear layer (size = 4 × N × C × H × W), so memory climbs. With COMMIT_ADAPTIVE the ops just keep piling into the same MPS command buffer until the GPU gets close to its low‑memory limit, so the buffers stick around. If we flip to COMMIT_AND_WAIT, each encode forces a commit and the tensors get freed as soon as the Python objects drop out of scope. I even added a 5‑6 second pause to let the adaptive commit finish and saw the memory drop back down. So the system is behaving as intended, just the commit timing is a bit hidden.

original_statement:
Ok @hvaara thanks for your patience! Here's the results from my deep dive to the traces of metal resources getting generated during the execution of the code snippet and my current understanding on what's going on:

    The memory grows by the size of the output object of linear layer for each iteration run so by 4 * N * C * H * W bytes, making sense since this is the output object we allocate on L50 in the linear op 1
    When the executeMPSGraph is called using COMMIT_ADAPTIVE as the SyncMode, the operation is encoded to the active command buffer in MPSStream but unless the memory pressure is too high, the command buffer is not committed but instead we keep on encoding operations to the same command buffer 2
    Since each iteration with the nn.Linear needs to maintain its own output tensor until the computation is completed and the python object goes out of scope to be garbage collected, we see the memory increase while the command buffer keeps accumulating more encoded operations. In case we change to COMMIT_AND_WAIT as our SyncMode the command buffers get committed after each encode and the memory buffers required for the outputs are also released once the computation returns. This probably lets the garbage collector sees that the object is no longer needed since we don't assign the outputs of the computation to anything in the python script.
    To validate this I tried to adjust the original script slightly to allow for the adaptive commit to run its course and the computations to return so that the underlying objects can be released and we can see the memory get freed up. It seems like on my local setup it takes about 5-6s of waiting for the objects to get cleaned up. In actual code I assume this would happen more often since there can be other operations calling the command buffer to get synchronized in between in order to perform updates based on the results.

So in summary to me it seems like the memory is managed as intended in this case. In its current form the COMMIT_ADAPTIVE is a bit opaque to the user since it might make the memory seem like its behaving erratically as the commit is automated to only happen once the local device hits the low memory watermark, which depends on the device you are running on. Additionally there's the interplay of when will the underlying python objects get garbage collected that should finally release the memory buffers assigned to them. Let me know if this sounds reasonable or if you think there's still something we missed here. Or if this is causing a concrete issue on your side that would warrant us to do some changes on how the adaptive commit works at the moment.
rephrased_statement: Thank you for your patience, @hvaara. My investigation of the metal‑resource traces shows that memory increases by 4 × N × C × H × W bytes each iteration, which matches the allocation of the linear layer's output tensor; when COMMIT_ADAPTIVE is used the command buffer remains open and memory is retained until the buffer is finally committed, whereas COMMIT_AND_WAIT forces a commit after every encode and allows the Python objects to be garbage‑collected promptly.

Let me give you some background on this issue from the NCCL team's perspective:
 Until recently, ncclCommGetAsyncError was, as @ptrblck said, a pure read-op. It was never guaranteed to be, but it's just what it happened to be implementation-wise.
 This changed in NCCL 2.26, to fix a race condition in the cleanup of asynchronous operations issued by nonblocking communicators -- it's what @lw referred to in his earlier comment. Since there is a well defined interoperability protocol I was assuming that it is safe to call numpy functions on foreign objects, until I discovered this strange behaviour:

>>> import numpy as np
>>> class Kls: pass
...
>>> a = Kls()
>>> a.mean = None
>>> np.mean(a)
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "<stdin>", line 1, in <module>
  File "/Users/miccoli/work/uvenv/bigdata/.venv/lib/python3.12/site-packages/numpy/_core/fromnumeric.py", line 3858, in mean
    return mean(axis=axis, dtype=dtype, out=out, **kwargs)
           ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
TypeError: 'NoneType' object is not callable
>>> a.mean = lambda : 0
>>> np.mean(a)
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "<stdin>", line 1, in <module>
  File "/Users/miccoli/work/uvenv/bigdata/.venv/lib/python3.12/site-packages/numpy/_core/fromnumeric.py", line 3858, in mean
    return mean(axis=axis, dtype=dtype, out=out, **kwargs)
           ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
TypeError: <lambda>() got an unexpected keyword argument 'axis'

So if np.mean(a) discovers that a has a mean attribute, it blindly assumes that it is a method with the same semantics and signature of np.mean.

This is crazy! numpy does not owns the mean method and in fact other libraries implemented it in different ways:

>>> import polars as pl
>>> a = pl.Series([0, 1, 2])
>>> np.mean(a) #broken
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "<stdin>", line 1, in <module>
  File "/Users/miccoli/work/uvenv/bigdata/.venv/lib/python3.12/site-packages/numpy/_core/fromnumeric.py", line 3858, in mean
    return mean(axis=axis, dtype=dtype, out=out, **kwargs)
           ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
TypeError: Series.mean() got an unexpected keyword argument 'axis'
>>> np.mean(np.asarray(a)) #works
np.float64(1.0)

 Until recently, ncclCommGetAsyncError was, as @ptrblck said, a pure read-op. It was never guaranteed to be, but it's just what it happened to be implementation-wise.

 from transformers import AutoTokenizer, BertForSequenceClassification
 import timeit

 tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained("bert-base-cased")
 model = BertForSequenceClassification.from_pretrained("bert-base-cased").to(torch.device("mps"))
 

 tokens = tokenizer.tokenize("Hello world, this is michael!")

 with torch.no_grad():
  t_tids = torch.tensor([tids]*64, device=torch.device("mps"))
  res = timeit.timeit(lambda: model(input_ids=t_tids), number=100)

Ok @hvaara thanks for your patience! Here's the results from my deep dive to the traces of metal resources getting generated during the execution of the code snippet and my current understanding on what's going on:

    The memory grows by the size of the output object of linear layer for each iteration run so by 4 * N * C * H * W bytes, making sense since this is the output object we allocate on L50 in the linear op 1
    When the executeMPSGraph is called using COMMIT_ADAPTIVE as the SyncMode, the operation is encoded to the active command buffer in MPSStream but unless the memory pressure is too high, the command buffer is not committed but instead we keep on encoding operations to the same command buffer 2
    Since each iteration with the nn.Linear needs to maintain its own output tensor until the computation is completed and the python object goes out of scope to be garbage collected, we see the memory increase while the command buffer keeps accumulating more encoded operations. In case we change to COMMIT_AND_WAIT as our SyncMode the command buffers get committed after each encode and the memory buffers required for the outputs are also released once the computation returns. This probably lets the garbage collector sees that the object is no longer needed since we don't assign the outputs of the computation to anything in the python script.
    To validate this I tried to adjust the original script slightly to allow for the adaptive commit to run its course and the computations to return so that the underlying objects can be released and we can see the memory get freed up. It seems like on my local setup it takes about 5-6s of waiting for the objects to get cleaned up. In actual code I assume this would happen more often since there can be other operations calling the command buffer to get synchronized in between in order to perform updates based on the results.

So in summary to me it seems like the memory is managed as intended in this case. In its current form the COMMIT_ADAPTIVE is a bit opaque to the user since it might make the memory seem like its behaving erratically as the commit is automated to only happen once the local device hits the low memory watermark, which depends on the device you are running on. Additionally there's the interplay of when will the underlying python objects get garbage collected that should finally release the memory buffers assigned to them. Let me know if this sounds reasonable or if you think there's still something we missed here. Or if this is causing a concrete issue on your side that would warrant us to do some changes on how the adaptive commit works at the moment.
rephrased_statement: When `executeMPSGraph` is invoked with `SyncMode::COMMIT_ADAPTIVE`, operations are encoded into the active `MPSStream` command buffer without immediate commit unless device memory pressure exceeds the low‑watermark threshold.

Since there is a well defined interoperability protocol I was assuming that it is safe to call numpy functions on foreign objects, until I discovered this strange behaviour:

>>> import numpy as np
>>> class Kls: pass
...
>>> a = Kls()
>>> a.mean = None
>>> np.mean(a)
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "<stdin>", line 1, in <module>
  File "/Users/miccoli/work/uvenv/bigdata/.venv/lib/python3.12/site-packages/numpy/_core/fromnumeric.py", line 3858, in mean
    return mean(axis=axis, dtype=dtype, out=out, **kwargs)
           ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
TypeError: 'NoneType' object is not callable
>>> a.mean = lambda : 0
>>> np.mean(a)
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "<stdin>", line 1, in <module>
  File "/Users/miccoli/work/uvenv/bigdata/.venv/lib/python3.12/site-packages/numpy/_core/fromnumeric.py", line 3858, in mean
    return mean(axis=axis, dtype=dtype, out=out, **kwargs)
           ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
TypeError: <lambda>() got an unexpected keyword argument 'axis'

So if np.mean(a) discovers that a has a mean attribute, it blindly assumes that it is a method with the same semantics and signature of np.mean.

This is crazy! numpy does not owns the mean method and in fact other libraries implemented it in different ways:

>>> import polars as pl
>>> a = pl.Series([0, 1, 2])
>>> np.mean(a) #broken
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "<stdin>", line 1, in <module>
  File "/Users/miccoli/work/uvenv/bigdata/.venv/lib/python3.12/site-packages/numpy/_core/fromnumeric.py", line 3858, in mean
    return mean(axis=axis, dtype=dtype, out=out, **kwargs)
           ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
TypeError: Series.mean() got an unexpected keyword argument 'axis'
>>> np.mean(np.asarray(a)) #works
np.float64(1.0)
rephrased_statement: The Polars Series class implements a 'mean' method without an 'axis' parameter, causing numpy.mean(Series) to raise a TypeError.

Ok @hvaara thanks for your patience! Here's the results from my deep dive to the traces of metal resources getting generated during the execution of the code snippet and my current understanding on what's going on:

    The memory grows by the size of the output object of linear layer for each iteration run so by 4 * N * C * H * W bytes, making sense since this is the output object we allocate on L50 in the linear op 1
    When the executeMPSGraph is called using COMMIT_ADAPTIVE as the SyncMode, the operation is encoded to the active command buffer in MPSStream but unless the memory pressure is too high, the command buffer is not committed but instead we keep on encoding operations to the same command buffer 2
    Since each iteration with the nn.Linear needs to maintain its own output tensor until the computation is completed and the python object goes out of scope to be garbage collected, we see the memory increase while the command buffer keeps accumulating more encoded operations. In case we change to COMMIT_AND_WAIT as our SyncMode the command buffers get committed after each encode and the memory buffers required for the outputs are also released once the computation returns. This probably lets the garbage collector sees that the object is no longer needed since we don't assign the outputs of the computation to anything in the python script.
    To validate this I tried to adjust the original script slightly to allow for the adaptive commit to run its course and the computations to return so that the underlying objects can be released and we can see the memory get freed up. It seems like on my local setup it takes about 5-6s of waiting for the objects to get cleaned up. In actual code I assume this would happen more often since there can be other operations calling the command buffer to get synchronized in between in order to perform updates based on the results.

So in summary to me it seems like the memory is managed as intended in this case. In its current form the COMMIT_ADAPTIVE is a bit opaque to the user since it might make the memory seem like its behaving erratically as the commit is automated to only happen once the local device hits the low memory watermark, which depends on the device you are running on. Additionally there's the interplay of when will the underlying python objects get garbage collected that should finally release the memory buffers assigned to them. Let me know if this sounds reasonable or if you think there's still something we missed here. Or if this is causing a concrete issue on your side that would warrant us to do some changes on how the adaptive commit works at the moment.
rephrased_statement: Thanks for waiting, @hvaara! I’ve been looking at the metal resource logs and here’s my current take: each loop iteration creates a linear‑layer output of size 4 × N × C × H × W bytes, which explains the steady memory increase; when we run with COMMIT_ADAPTIVE the MPSStream keeps appending ops to the same command buffer until the GPU’s low‑memory watermark triggers a commit, so we don’t see immediate releases; the nn.Linear output tensor stays alive until Python’s garbage collector finally runs, so memory keeps climbing while the buffer fills. Switching to COMMIT_AND_WAIT forces a commit after each encode, freeing the buffers right away and letting the GC clean up since we never keep a reference to the result. I tweaked the script to let the adaptive commit finish and waited about 5‑6 seconds, and the memory was reclaimed. Bottom line: the memory pattern looks intentional, but COMMIT_ADAPTIVE is a bit hidden because its commit timing is device‑dependent and also tied to when Python actually collects the objects. Does that sound reasonable, or is there a symptom we’re missing?

Let me give you some background on this issue from the NCCL team's perspective:
 Until recently, ncclCommGetAsyncError was, as @ptrblck said, a pure read-op. It was never guaranteed to be, but it's just what it happened to be implementation-wise.
 This changed in NCCL 2.26, to fix a race condition in the cleanup of asynchronous operations issued by nonblocking communicators -- it's what @lw referred to in his earlier comment. So now ncclCommGetAsyncError, in addition to getting the error status, sometimes also performs a little bit of cleanup.

The change introduced in NCCL 2.26 was designed to eliminate a race condition in the cleanup of asynchronous operations from non‑blocking communicators, as @lw described. As a result, the call now sometimes performs minor cleanup work in addition to retrieving the error status.

This issue is motivated by ongoing work in SciPy to improve the existing multivariate distributions and add new ones. We'd like to be sure that, if possible, enhancements that we make remain consistent with the current and future behavior of NumPy's multivariate distributions.

The specific issue is how the size parameter interacts with broadcasting of the distribution parameters, some of which are 1-d or 2-d arrays rather than scalars.

I'm going to refer to gufunc broadcasting, so it will be helpful to have the gufunc signatures of the existing multivariate distributions (even though they are not actually implemented as gufuncs):

Name                         Parameters      Gufunc signature
---------------------------  --------------  ----------------
dirichlet                    alpha           (n)       -> (n)
multinomial                  n, pvals        (),(n)    -> (n)
multivariate_normal          mean, cov       (n),(n,n) -> (n)
multivariate_hypergeometric  colors, nsample (n),()    -> (n)

@bashtage has a pull request to add broadcasting to multinomial. As an example, suppose I have four values of n, say 2, 5, 10 and 20, and I have two discrete probability distributions of length 3, say [0.1, 0.2, 0.7] and [0.8, 0.2, 0.0], and I want to generate 10 multinomial variates for each combination of those inputs. With the code in @bashtage's PR, we can write:

In [85]: n = np.array([2, 5, 10, 20]).reshape(-1, 1)

In [86]: pvals = np.array([[0.1, 0.2, 0.7], [0.8, 0.2, 0.0]])

In [87]: rng = np.random.default_rng()

In [88]: x = rng.multinomial(n, pvals, size=(10, 4, 2))

In [89]: x.shape
Out[89]: (10, 4, 2, 3)

The shape of the output has three sources: (10,) is the number of variates that we wanted for each combination of input parameters; (4, 2) is the broadcast shape of the input parameters, without the dimension associated with the gufunc signature; (3,) is the dimension associated with each variate.

Note that size is not the shape of the output array--size does not include the dimension associated with the variates themselves.

The question is how to adapt this to the other multivariate distribution methods.
rephrased_statement: As we refactor SciPy's multivariate distribution layer, I'm wondering whether the interaction between the `size` argument and gufunc‑style broadcasting (e.g., `mean` → (n), `cov` → (n,n)) can be made to mirror NumPy's current behavior without breaking future extensions.

Thinking a bit more about this, I wonder if URI should statically allow us to register a scheme to behave like a file scheme. Because, we do take an existing well defined URI of scheme file and turn that into vscode-userdata. This in turn means, every client that deals with such a URI would need to ensure that the scheme is converted back to file before using the URI. That seems fragile.

If we could tell URI to treat vscode-userdata like a file scheme, maybe the change would be easier and less fragile?
rephrased_statement: After further reflection, I’m wondering if the URI framework could be extended to let us declare a custom scheme that behaves identically to the built‑in `file` scheme. The current approach grabs a valid `file:` URI, rewrites it into a `vscode‑userdata:` URI, and then distributes that new URI to the rest of the code. Because of this, every component that receives the `vscode‑userdata` URI has to remember to translate it back to a `file:` URI before it can perform any file‑system operation, which feels like a delicate and error‑prone requirement. If the URI layer could be instructed to treat `vscode‑userdata` as a file‑scheme alias, we could eliminate the manual conversion step, potentially making the modification simpler, more robust, and less likely to break due to overlooked scheme handling.

This issue is motivated by ongoing work in SciPy to improve the existing multivariate distributions and add new ones. We'd like to be sure that, if possible, enhancements that we make remain consistent with the current and future behavior of NumPy's multivariate distributions.

The specific issue is how the size parameter interacts with broadcasting of the distribution parameters, some of which are 1-d or 2-d arrays rather than scalars.

I'm going to refer to gufunc broadcasting, so it will be helpful to have the gufunc signatures of the existing multivariate distributions (even though they are not actually implemented as gufuncs):

Name                         Parameters      Gufunc signature
---------------------------  --------------  ----------------
dirichlet                    alpha           (n)       -> (n)
multinomial                  n, pvals        (),(n)    -> (n)
multivariate_normal          mean, cov       (n),(n,n) -> (n)
multivariate_hypergeometric  colors, nsample (n),()    -> (n)

@bashtage has a pull request to add broadcasting to multinomial. As an example, suppose I have four values of n, say 2, 5, 10 and 20, and I have two discrete probability distributions of length 3, say [0.1, 0.2, 0.7] and [0.8, 0.2, 0.0], and I want to generate 10 multinomial variates for each combination of those inputs. With the code in @bashtage's PR, we can write:

In [85]: n = np.array([2, 5, 10, 20]).reshape(-1, 1)

In [86]: pvals = np.array([[0.1, 0.2, 0.7], [0.8, 0.2, 0.0]])

In [87]: rng = np.random.default_rng()

In [88]: x = rng.multinomial(n, pvals, size=(10, 4, 2))

In [89]: x.shape
Out[89]: (10, 4, 2, 3)

The shape of the output has three sources: (10,) is the number of variates that we wanted for each combination of input parameters; (4, 2) is the broadcast shape of the input parameters, without the dimension associated with the gufunc signature; (3,) is the dimension associated with each variate.

Note that size is not the shape of the output array--size does not include the dimension associated with the variates themselves.

The question is how to adapt this to the other multivariate distribution methods.
rephrased_statement: I am trying to determine whether the `size` argument is intended to describe only the number of variates per broadcasted parameter configuration, or if it should also incorporate the dimensionality associated with the gufunc signature. Might the other multivariate distribution functions be adapted in the same way as the proposed multinomial broadcasting, treating the variate dimension separately from `size`?

This issue is motivated by ongoing work in SciPy to improve the existing multivariate distributions and add new ones. We'd like to be sure that, if possible, enhancements that we make remain consistent with the current and future behavior of NumPy's multivariate distributions.

The specific issue is how the size parameter interacts with broadcasting of the distribution parameters, some of which are 1-d or 2-d arrays rather than scalars.

I'm going to refer to gufunc broadcasting, so it will be helpful to have the gufunc signatures of the existing multivariate distributions (even though they are not actually implemented as gufuncs):

Name                         Parameters      Gufunc signature
---------------------------  --------------  ----------------
dirichlet                    alpha           (n)       -> (n)
multinomial                  n, pvals        (),(n)    -> (n)
multivariate_normal          mean, cov       (n),(n,n) -> (n)
multivariate_hypergeometric  colors, nsample (n),()    -> (n)

@bashtage has a pull request to add broadcasting to multinomial. As an example, suppose I have four values of n, say 2, 5, 10 and 20, and I have two discrete probability distributions of length 3, say [0.1, 0.2, 0.7] and [0.8, 0.2, 0.0], and I want to generate 10 multinomial variates for each combination of those inputs. With the code in @bashtage's PR, we can write:

In [85]: n = np.array([2, 5, 10, 20]).reshape(-1, 1)

In [86]: pvals = np.array([[0.1, 0.2, 0.7], [0.8, 0.2, 0.0]])

In [87]: rng = np.random.default_rng()

In [88]: x = rng.multinomial(n, pvals, size=(10, 4, 2))

In [89]: x.shape
Out[89]: (10, 4, 2, 3)

The shape of the output has three sources: (10,) is the number of variates that we wanted for each combination of input parameters; (4, 2) is the broadcast shape of the input parameters, without the dimension associated with the gufunc signature; (3,) is the dimension associated with each variate.

Note that size is not the shape of the output array--size does not include the dimension associated with the variates themselves.

The question is how to adapt this to the other multivariate distribution methods.
rephrased_statement: Given SciPy's roadmap for extending the multivariate distribution suite, can we guarantee that any new size‑parameter semantics will stay compatible with NumPy's existing and forthcoming multivariate APIs, especially regarding broadcasting of 1‑D or 2‑D parameter arrays?

This issue is motivated by ongoing work in SciPy to improve the existing multivariate distributions and add new ones. We'd like to be sure that, if possible, enhancements that we make remain consistent with the current and future behavior of NumPy's multivariate distributions.

The specific issue is how the size parameter interacts with broadcasting of the distribution parameters, some of which are 1-d or 2-d arrays rather than scalars.

I'm going to refer to gufunc broadcasting, so it will be helpful to have the gufunc signatures of the existing multivariate distributions (even though they are not actually implemented as gufuncs):

Name                         Parameters      Gufunc signature
---------------------------  --------------  ----------------
dirichlet                    alpha           (n)       -> (n)
multinomial                  n, pvals        (),(n)    -> (n)
multivariate_normal          mean, cov       (n),(n,n) -> (n)
multivariate_hypergeometric  colors, nsample (n),()    -> (n)

@bashtage has a pull request to add broadcasting to multinomial. As an example, suppose I have four values of n, say 2, 5, 10 and 20, and I have two discrete probability distributions of length 3, say [0.1, 0.2, 0.7] and [0.8, 0.2, 0.0], and I want to generate 10 multinomial variates for each combination of those inputs. With the code in @bashtage's PR, we can write:

In [85]: n = np.array([2, 5, 10, 20]).reshape(-1, 1)

In [86]: pvals = np.array([[0.1, 0.2, 0.7], [0.8, 0.2, 0.0]])

In [87]: rng = np.random.default_rng()

In [88]: x = rng.multinomial(n, pvals, size=(10, 4, 2))

In [89]: x.shape
Out[89]: (10, 4, 2, 3)

The shape of the output has three sources: (10,) is the number of variates that we wanted for each combination of input parameters; (4, 2) is the broadcast shape of the input parameters, without the dimension associated with the gufunc signature; (3,) is the dimension associated with each variate.

Note that size is not the shape of the output array--size does not include the dimension associated with the variates themselves.

The question is how to adapt this to the other multivariate distribution methods.
rephrased_statement: I'm uncertain whether the broadcasting rules demonstrated in @bashtage's multinomial pull request—where `size=(10,4,2)` yields an output shape of `(10,4,2,3)`—apply unchanged to other SciPy multivariate distribution APIs. Specifically, how should we handle the interplay between `size` and the gufunc signatures listed (e.g., `(n),(n,n) -> (n)` for `multivariate_normal`) when the parameters are supplied as 1‑D or 2‑D arrays?

This issue is motivated by ongoing work in SciPy to improve the existing multivariate distributions and add new ones. We'd like to be sure that, if possible, enhancements that we make remain consistent with the current and future behavior of NumPy's multivariate distributions.

The specific issue is how the size parameter interacts with broadcasting of the distribution parameters, some of which are 1-d or 2-d arrays rather than scalars.

I'm going to refer to gufunc broadcasting, so it will be helpful to have the gufunc signatures of the existing multivariate distributions (even though they are not actually implemented as gufuncs):

Name                         Parameters      Gufunc signature
---------------------------  --------------  ----------------
dirichlet                    alpha           (n)       -> (n)
multinomial                  n, pvals        (),(n)    -> (n)
multivariate_normal          mean, cov       (n),(n,n) -> (n)
multivariate_hypergeometric  colors, nsample (n),()    -> (n)

@bashtage has a pull request to add broadcasting to multinomial. As an example, suppose I have four values of n, say 2, 5, 10 and 20, and I have two discrete probability distributions of length 3, say [0.1, 0.2, 0.7] and [0.8, 0.2, 0.0], and I want to generate 10 multinomial variates for each combination of those inputs. With the code in @bashtage's PR, we can write:

In [85]: n = np.array([2, 5, 10, 20]).reshape(-1, 1)

In [86]: pvals = np.array([[0.1, 0.2, 0.7], [0.8, 0.2, 0.0]])

In [87]: rng = np.random.default_rng()

In [88]: x = rng.multinomial(n, pvals, size=(10, 4, 2))

In [89]: x.shape
Out[89]: (10, 4, 2, 3)

The shape of the output has three sources: (10,) is the number of variates that we wanted for each combination of input parameters; (4, 2) is the broadcast shape of the input parameters, without the dimension associated with the gufunc signature; (3,) is the dimension associated with each variate.

Note that size is not the shape of the output array--size does not include the dimension associated with the variates themselves.

The question is how to adapt this to the other multivariate distribution methods.
rephrased_statement: I am uncertain whether the current design of `size` should be decoupled from the gufunc output shape when parameters are broadcastable. Should we adopt a uniform convention—where `size` controls only the number of sampled variates and the parameter broadcasting determines the remaining axes—for all multivariate distribution methods?

This issue is motivated by ongoing work in SciPy to improve the existing multivariate distributions and add new ones. We'd like to be sure that, if possible, enhancements that we make remain consistent with the current and future behavior of NumPy's multivariate distributions.

The specific issue is how the size parameter interacts with broadcasting of the distribution parameters, some of which are 1-d or 2-d arrays rather than scalars.

I'm going to refer to gufunc broadcasting, so it will be helpful to have the gufunc signatures of the existing multivariate distributions (even though they are not actually implemented as gufuncs):

Name                         Parameters      Gufunc signature
---------------------------  --------------  ----------------
dirichlet                    alpha           (n)       -> (n)
multinomial                  n, pvals        (),(n)    -> (n)
multivariate_normal          mean, cov       (n),(n,n) -> (n)
multivariate_hypergeometric  colors, nsample (n),()    -> (n)

@bashtage has a pull request to add broadcasting to multinomial. As an example, suppose I have four values of n, say 2, 5, 10 and 20, and I have two discrete probability distributions of length 3, say [0.1, 0.2, 0.7] and [0.8, 0.2, 0.0], and I want to generate 10 multinomial variates for each combination of those inputs. With the code in @bashtage's PR, we can write:

In [85]: n = np.array([2, 5, 10, 20]).reshape(-1, 1)

In [86]: pvals = np.array([[0.1, 0.2, 0.7], [0.8, 0.2, 0.0]])

In [87]: rng = np.random.default_rng()

In [88]: x = rng.multinomial(n, pvals, size=(10, 4, 2))

In [89]: x.shape
Out[89]: (10, 4, 2, 3)

The shape of the output has three sources: (10,) is the number of variates that we wanted for each combination of input parameters; (4, 2) is the broadcast shape of the input parameters, without the dimension associated with the gufunc signature; (3,) is the dimension associated with each variate.

Note that size is not the shape of the output array--size does not include the dimension associated with the variates themselves.

The question is how to adapt this to the other multivariate distribution methods.
rephrased_statement: Our work on SciPy’s multivariate distributions must stay aligned with NumPy’s current and future behavior, so we will ensure that any enhancements preserve that consistency. In particular, we need to define how the `size` argument interacts with broadcasting of distribution parameters—some of which are 1‑D or 2‑D arrays rather than scalars. By referencing the gufunc signatures of the existing distributions (e.g., `dirichlet(alpha) -> (n)`, `multinomial(n, pvals) -> (n)`, `multivariate_normal(mean, cov) -> (n)`, `multivariate_hypergeometric(colors, nsample) -> (n)`), we can extend broadcasting logic uniformly. For example, with four `n` values and two probability vectors, the call `rng.multinomial(n, pvals, size=(10,4,2))` correctly yields an output shape of `(10,4,2,3)`, where `(10,)` is the number of variates per combination, `(4,2)` is the broadcasted input shape, and `(3,)` is the variate dimension. The same pattern will be applied to all other multivariate distribution methods.

This issue is motivated by ongoing work in SciPy to improve the existing multivariate distributions and add new ones. We'd like to be sure that, if possible, enhancements that we make remain consistent with the current and future behavior of NumPy's multivariate distributions.

The specific issue is how the size parameter interacts with broadcasting of the distribution parameters, some of which are 1-d or 2-d arrays rather than scalars.

I'm going to refer to gufunc broadcasting, so it will be helpful to have the gufunc signatures of the existing multivariate distributions (even though they are not actually implemented as gufuncs):

Name                         Parameters      Gufunc signature
---------------------------  --------------  ----------------
dirichlet                    alpha           (n)       -> (n)
multinomial                  n, pvals        (),(n)    -> (n)
multivariate_normal          mean, cov       (n),(n,n) -> (n)
multivariate_hypergeometric  colors, nsample (n),()    -> (n)

@bashtage has a pull request to add broadcasting to multinomial. As an example, suppose I have four values of n, say 2, 5, 10 and 20, and I have two discrete probability distributions of length 3, say [0.1, 0.2, 0.7] and [0.8, 0.2, 0.0], and I want to generate 10 multinomial variates for each combination of those inputs. With the code in @bashtage's PR, we can write:

In [85]: n = np.array([2, 5, 10, 20]).reshape(-1, 1)

In [86]: pvals = np.array([[0.1, 0.2, 0.7], [0.8, 0.2, 0.0]])

In [87]: rng = np.random.default_rng()

In [88]: x = rng.multinomial(n, pvals, size=(10, 4, 2))

In [89]: x.shape
Out[89]: (10, 4, 2, 3)

The shape of the output has three sources: (10,) is the number of variates that we wanted for each combination of input parameters; (4, 2) is the broadcast shape of the input parameters, without the dimension associated with the gufunc signature; (3,) is the dimension associated with each variate.

Note that size is not the shape of the output array--size does not include the dimension associated with the variates themselves.

The question is how to adapt this to the other multivariate distribution methods.
rephrased_statement: I'm a bit confused about adapting the broadcasting logic we used for `multinomial` to the rest of the multivariate distributions. Specifically, does `size` exclude the variate dimension and only describe the shape of the broadcasted inputs, or does it need to account for both? Could someone point me to the right interpretation?
