This issue is motivated by ongoing work in SciPy to improve the existing multivariate distributions and add new ones. We'd like to be sure that, if possible, enhancements that we make remain consistent with the current and future behavior of NumPy's multivariate distributions.

The specific issue is how the size parameter interacts with broadcasting of the distribution parameters, some of which are 1-d or 2-d arrays rather than scalars.

I'm going to refer to gufunc broadcasting, so it will be helpful to have the gufunc signatures of the existing multivariate distributions (even though they are not actually implemented as gufuncs):

Name                         Parameters      Gufunc signature
---------------------------  --------------  ----------------
dirichlet                    alpha           (n)       -> (n)
multinomial                  n, pvals        (),(n)    -> (n)
multivariate_normal          mean, cov       (n),(n,n) -> (n)
multivariate_hypergeometric  colors, nsample (n),()    -> (n)

@bashtage has a pull request to add broadcasting to multinomial. As an example, suppose I have four values of n, say 2, 5, 10 and 20, and I have two discrete probability distributions of length 3, say [0.1, 0.2, 0.7] and [0.8, 0.2, 0.0], and I want to generate 10 multinomial variates for each combination of those inputs. With the code in @bashtage's PR, we can write:

In [85]: n = np.array([2, 5, 10, 20]).reshape(-1, 1)

In [86]: pvals = np.array([[0.1, 0.2, 0.7], [0.8, 0.2, 0.0]])

In [87]: rng = np.random.default_rng()

In [88]: x = rng.multinomial(n, pvals, size=(10, 4, 2))

In [89]: x.shape
Out[89]: (10, 4, 2, 3)

The shape of the output has three sources: (10,) is the number of variates that we wanted for each combination of input parameters; (4, 2) is the broadcast shape of the input parameters, without the dimension associated with the gufunc signature; (3,) is the dimension associated with each variate.

Note that size is not the shape of the output array--size does not include the dimension associated with the variates themselves.

The question is how to adapt this to the other multivariate distribution methods.
rephrased_statement: Quick question: when we add broadcasting support to the other multivariate distribution methods, should the `size` kwarg reflect only the number of draws we want, or also the broadcasted shape of the input parameters (like the `(4,2)` part in the multinomial example)? I'm not clear on the expected semantics.

This issue is motivated by ongoing work in SciPy to improve the existing multivariate distributions and add new ones. We'd like to be sure that, if possible, enhancements that we make remain consistent with the current and future behavior of NumPy's multivariate distributions.

The specific issue is how the size parameter interacts with broadcasting of the distribution parameters, some of which are 1-d or 2-d arrays rather than scalars.

I'm going to refer to gufunc broadcasting, so it will be helpful to have the gufunc signatures of the existing multivariate distributions (even though they are not actually implemented as gufuncs):

Name                         Parameters      Gufunc signature
---------------------------  --------------  ----------------
dirichlet                    alpha           (n)       -> (n)
multinomial                  n, pvals        (),(n)    -> (n)
multivariate_normal          mean, cov       (n),(n,n) -> (n)
multivariate_hypergeometric  colors, nsample (n),()    -> (n)

@bashtage has a pull request to add broadcasting to multinomial. As an example, suppose I have four values of n, say 2, 5, 10 and 20, and I have two discrete probability distributions of length 3, say [0.1, 0.2, 0.7] and [0.8, 0.2, 0.0], and I want to generate 10 multinomial variates for each combination of those inputs. With the code in @bashtage's PR, we can write:

In [85]: n = np.array([2, 5, 10, 20]).reshape(-1, 1)

In [86]: pvals = np.array([[0.1, 0.2, 0.7], [0.8, 0.2, 0.0]])

In [87]: rng = np.random.default_rng()

In [88]: x = rng.multinomial(n, pvals, size=(10, 4, 2))

In [89]: x.shape
Out[89]: (10, 4, 2, 3)

The shape of the output has three sources: (10,) is the number of variates that we wanted for each combination of input parameters; (4, 2) is the broadcast shape of the input parameters, without the dimension associated with the gufunc signature; (3,) is the dimension associated with each variate.

Note that size is not the shape of the output array--size does not include the dimension associated with the variates themselves.

The question is how to adapt this to the other multivariate distribution methods.
rephrased_statement: The compatibility of SciPy's multivariate distribution enhancements with NumPy's current and future semantics hinges on correctly handling the `size` parameter alongside broadcasting of non‑scalar parameters.

Using MPS for BERT inference appears to produce about a 2x slowdown compared to the CPU. Here is code to reproduce the issue:
 # MPS Version
 from transformers import AutoTokenizer, BertForSequenceClassification
 import timeit
 import torch
 

 tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained("bert-base-cased")
 model = BertForSequenceClassification.from_pretrained("bert-base-cased").to(torch.device("mps"))

 CUDA 0.82 s

This issue is motivated by ongoing work in SciPy to improve the existing multivariate distributions and add new ones. We'd like to be sure that, if possible, enhancements that we make remain consistent with the current and future behavior of NumPy's multivariate distributions.

The specific issue is how the size parameter interacts with broadcasting of the distribution parameters, some of which are 1-d or 2-d arrays rather than scalars.

I'm going to refer to gufunc broadcasting, so it will be helpful to have the gufunc signatures of the existing multivariate distributions (even though they are not actually implemented as gufuncs):

Name                         Parameters      Gufunc signature
---------------------------  --------------  ----------------
dirichlet                    alpha           (n)       -> (n)
multinomial                  n, pvals        (),(n)    -> (n)
multivariate_normal          mean, cov       (n),(n,n) -> (n)

I'm going to refer to gufunc broadcasting, so it will be helpful to have the gufunc signatures of the existing multivariate distributions (even though they are not actually implemented as gufuncs):

Name                         Parameters      Gufunc signature
---------------------------  --------------  ----------------
dirichlet                    alpha           (n)       -> (n)
multinomial                  n, pvals        (),(n)    -> (n)
multivariate_normal          mean, cov       (n),(n,n) -> (n)
multivariate_hypergeometric  colors, nsample (n),()    -> (n)

@bashtage has a pull request to add broadcasting to multinomial. As an example, suppose I have four values of n, say 2, 5, 10 and 20, and I have two discrete probability distributions of length 3, say [0.1, 0.2, 0.7] and [0.8, 0.2, 0.0], and I want to generate 10 multinomial variates for each combination of those inputs. In [86]: pvals = np.array([[0.1, 0.2, 0.7], [0.8, 0.2, 0.0]])

In [87]: rng = np.random.default_rng()

In [88]: x = rng.multinomial(n, pvals, size=(10, 4, 2))

In [89]: x.shape
Out[89]: (10, 4, 2, 3)

The shape of the output has three sources: (10,) is the number of variates that we wanted for each combination of input parameters; (4, 2) is the broadcast shape of the input parameters, without the dimension associated with the gufunc signature; (3,) is the dimension associated with each variate.

Note that size is not the shape of the output array--size does not include the dimension associated with the variates themselves.

The question is how to adapt this to the other multivariate distribution methods.

original_statement:
This issue is motivated by ongoing work in SciPy to improve the existing multivariate distributions and add new ones. We'd like to be sure that, if possible, enhancements that we make remain consistent with the current and future behavior of NumPy's multivariate distributions.

The specific issue is how the size parameter interacts with broadcasting of the distribution parameters, some of which are 1-d or 2-d arrays rather than scalars.

I'm going to refer to gufunc broadcasting, so it will be helpful to have the gufunc signatures of the existing multivariate distributions (even though they are not actually implemented as gufuncs):

Name                         Parameters      Gufunc signature
---------------------------  --------------  ----------------
dirichlet                    alpha           (n)       -> (n)
multinomial                  n, pvals        (),(n)    -> (n)
multivariate_normal          mean, cov       (n),(n,n) -> (n)
multivariate_hypergeometric  colors, nsample (n),()    -> (n)

@bashtage has a pull request to add broadcasting to multinomial. As an example, suppose I have four values of n, say 2, 5, 10 and 20, and I have two discrete probability distributions of length 3, say [0.1, 0.2, 0.7] and [0.8, 0.2, 0.0], and I want to generate 10 multinomial variates for each combination of those inputs. With the code in @bashtage's PR, we can write:

In [85]: n = np.array([2, 5, 10, 20]).reshape(-1, 1)

In [86]: pvals = np.array([[0.1, 0.2, 0.7], [0.8, 0.2, 0.0]])

In [87]: rng = np.random.default_rng()

In [88]: x = rng.multinomial(n, pvals, size=(10, 4, 2))

In [89]: x.shape
Out[89]: (10, 4, 2, 3)

The shape of the output has three sources: (10,) is the number of variates that we wanted for each combination of input parameters; (4, 2) is the broadcast shape of the input parameters, without the dimension associated with the gufunc signature; (3,) is the dimension associated with each variate.

Note that size is not the shape of the output array--size does not include the dimension associated with the variates themselves.

The question is how to adapt this to the other multivariate distribution methods.
rephrased_statement: Just to give some context: SciPy is trying to extend its multivariate distributions while staying compatible with NumPy's current and future behavior. The tricky part is figuring out how the `size` argument should behave when the distribution parameters themselves get broadcast (e.g., some are vectors, some are matrices). We have a concrete example for `multinomial` that shows `size=(10,4,2)` produces an output shape of `(10,4,2,3)`, where the last dimension comes from the gufunc signature. I'm wondering how we should generalize this pattern to `dirichlet`, `multivariate_normal`, and `multivariate_hypergeometric`.

 import timeit

 tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained("bert-base-cased")

Since there is a well defined interoperability protocol I was assuming that it is safe to call numpy functions on foreign objects, until I discovered this strange behaviour:

>>> import numpy as np
>>> class Kls: pass
...
>>> a = Kls()
>>> a.mean = None
>>> np.mean(a)
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "<stdin>", line 1, in <module>
  File "/Users/miccoli/work/uvenv/bigdata/.venv/lib/python3.12/site-packages/numpy/_core/fromnumeric.py", line 3858, in mean
    return mean(axis=axis, dtype=dtype, out=out, **kwargs)
           ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
TypeError: 'NoneType' object is not callable
>>> a.mean = lambda : 0
>>> np.mean(a)
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "<stdin>", line 1, in <module>
  File "/Users/miccoli/work/uvenv/bigdata/.venv/lib/python3.12/site-packages/numpy/_core/fromnumeric.py", line 3858, in mean
    return mean(axis=axis, dtype=dtype, out=out, **kwargs)
           ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
TypeError: <lambda>() got an unexpected keyword argument 'axis'

So if np.mean(a) discovers that a has a mean attribute, it blindly assumes that it is a method with the same semantics and signature of np.mean.

This is crazy! numpy does not owns the mean method and in fact other libraries implemented it in different ways:

>>> import polars as pl
>>> a = pl.Series([0, 1, 2])
>>> np.mean(a) #broken
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "<stdin>", line 1, in <module>
  File "/Users/miccoli/work/uvenv/bigdata/.venv/lib/python3.12/site-packages/numpy/_core/fromnumeric.py", line 3858, in mean
    return mean(axis=axis, dtype=dtype, out=out, **kwargs)
           ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
TypeError: Series.mean() got an unexpected keyword argument 'axis'
>>> np.mean(np.asarray(a)) #works
np.float64(1.0)
rephrased_statement:
I figured the NumPy interop spec meant I could safely call its functions on any object that looked like it had the right attributes, but I just discovered a bizarre edge case:
```python
class Kls: pass

a = Kls()
a.mean = None
np.mean(a)  # TypeError: 'NoneType' object is not callable

a.mean = lambda: 0
np.mean(a)  # TypeError: <lambda>() got an unexpected keyword argument 'axis'
```
Turns out `np.mean` inspects the object, sees a `mean` attribute, and then calls it as if it were NumPy’s own implementation, expecting the same `axis`, `dtype`, and `out` parameters. When the attribute is just a placeholder or a lambda with a different signature, NumPy crashes. The same thing happens with Polars—`np.mean(pl.Series([0,1,2]))` raises a `TypeError` because Polars’ `Series.mean()` doesn’t accept `axis`. Only after converting to a NumPy array does it behave as expected. I’m absolutely certain this is a hidden gotcha that the docs don’t mention.

This issue is motivated by ongoing work in SciPy to improve the existing multivariate distributions and add new ones. We'd like to be sure that, if possible, enhancements that we make remain consistent with the current and future behavior of NumPy's multivariate distributions.

The specific issue is how the size parameter interacts with broadcasting of the distribution parameters, some of which are 1-d or 2-d arrays rather than scalars.

I'm going to refer to gufunc broadcasting, so it will be helpful to have the gufunc signatures of the existing multivariate distributions (even though they are not actually implemented as gufuncs):

Name                         Parameters      Gufunc signature
---------------------------  --------------  ----------------
dirichlet                    alpha           (n)       -> (n)
multinomial                  n, pvals        (),(n)    -> (n)
multivariate_normal          mean, cov       (n),(n,n) -> (n)
multivariate_hypergeometric  colors, nsample (n),()    -> (n)

@bashtage has a pull request to add broadcasting to multinomial. As an example, suppose I have four values of n, say 2, 5, 10 and 20, and I have two discrete probability distributions of length 3, say [0.1, 0.2, 0.7] and [0.8, 0.2, 0.0], and I want to generate 10 multinomial variates for each combination of those inputs. With the code in @bashtage's PR, we can write:

In [85]: n = np.array([2, 5, 10, 20]).reshape(-1, 1)

In [86]: pvals = np.array([[0.1, 0.2, 0.7], [0.8, 0.2, 0.0]])

In [87]: rng = np.random.default_rng()

In [88]: x = rng.multinomial(n, pvals, size=(10, 4, 2))

In [89]: x.shape
Out[89]: (10, 4, 2, 3)

The shape of the output has three sources: (10,) is the number of variates that we wanted for each combination of input parameters; (4, 2) is the broadcast shape of the input parameters, without the dimension associated with the gufunc signature; (3,) is the dimension associated with each variate.

Note that size is not the shape of the output array--size does not include the dimension associated with the variates themselves.

The question is how to adapt this to the other multivariate distribution methods.
rephrased_statement:
We will ensure that any improvements to SciPy’s multivariate distributions remain in lockstep with NumPy’s behavior by formalizing the interaction between the `size` parameter and broadcasting of distribution parameters. The relevant gufunc signatures—`dirichlet(alpha) -> (n)`, `multinomial(n, pvals) -> (n)`, `multivariate_normal(mean, cov) -> (n)`, `multivariate_hypergeometric(colors, nsample) -> (n)`—serve as the blueprint. For example, using
```python
n = np.array([2,5,10,20]).reshape(-1,1)
pvals = np.array([[0.1,0.2,0.7],[0.8,0.2,0.0]])
rng = np.random.default_rng()
result = rng.multinomial(n, pvals, size=(10,4,2))
```
produces an output shape of `(10,4,2,3)`, where the first dimension is the number of variates per parameter combination, the next two dimensions are the broadcasted input shape, and the final dimension is the size of each variate. This broadcasting strategy will be consistently applied to all other multivariate distribution functions.

This issue is motivated by ongoing work in SciPy to improve the existing multivariate distributions and add new ones. We'd like to be sure that, if possible, enhancements that we make remain consistent with the current and future behavior of NumPy's multivariate distributions.

The specific issue is how the size parameter interacts with broadcasting of the distribution parameters, some of which are 1-d or 2-d arrays rather than scalars.

I'm going to refer to gufunc broadcasting, so it will be helpful to have the gufunc signatures of the existing multivariate distributions (even though they are not actually implemented as gufuncs):

Name                         Parameters      Gufunc signature
---------------------------  --------------  ----------------
dirichlet                    alpha           (n)       -> (n)
multinomial                  n, pvals        (),(n)    -> (n)
multivariate_normal          mean, cov       (n),(n,n) -> (n)
multivariate_hypergeometric  colors, nsample (n),()    -> (n)

@bashtage has a pull request to add broadcasting to multinomial. As an example, suppose I have four values of n, say 2, 5, 10 and 20, and I have two discrete probability distributions of length 3, say [0.1, 0.2, 0.7] and [0.8, 0.2, 0.0], and I want to generate 10 multinomial variates for each combination of those inputs. With the code in @bashtage's PR, we can write:

In [85]: n = np.array([2, 5, 10, 20]).reshape(-1, 1)

In [86]: pvals = np.array([[0.1, 0.2, 0.7], [0.8, 0.2, 0.0]])

In [87]: rng = np.random.default_rng()

In [88]: x = rng.multinomial(n, pvals, size=(10, 4, 2))

In [89]: x.shape
Out[89]: (10, 4, 2, 3)

The shape of the output has three sources: (10,) is the number of variates that we wanted for each combination of input parameters; (4, 2) is the broadcast shape of the input parameters, without the dimension associated with the gufunc signature; (3,) is the dimension associated with each variate.

Note that size is not the shape of the output array--size does not include the dimension associated with the variates themselves.

The question is how to adapt this to the other multivariate distribution methods.
rephrased_statement: Hey folks, as part of the ongoing SciPy effort to polish up our multivariate distributions and roll out a few new ones, we need to double‑check that any changes we make stay in step with NumPy's current and upcoming multivariate distribution API. The sticking point right now is the `size` argument: it seems to get tangled up with broadcasting when the distribution parameters are arrays (think 1‑D or 2‑D) instead of simple scalars. To get a handle on this, I'm looking at the gufunc‑style signatures for each distribution – e.g., `multivariate_normal` is `(n),(n,n) -> (n)` – even though they're not actual gufuncs yet. The PR by @bashtage adds broadcasting support to `multinomial`, letting you do something like `rng.multinomial(n, pvals, size=(10,4,2))` and get an output shape of `(10,4,2,3)`. The challenge now is to extend that broadcasting behavior to the other multivariate distribution functions so that `size` cleanly specifies the number of samples without accidentally adding extra dimensions from the parameter shapes.

This issue is motivated by ongoing work in SciPy to improve the existing multivariate distributions and add new ones. We'd like to be sure that, if possible, enhancements that we make remain consistent with the current and future behavior of NumPy's multivariate distributions.

The specific issue is how the size parameter interacts with broadcasting of the distribution parameters, some of which are 1-d or 2-d arrays rather than scalars.

I'm going to refer to gufunc broadcasting, so it will be helpful to have the gufunc signatures of the existing multivariate distributions (even though they are not actually implemented as gufuncs):

Name                         Parameters      Gufunc signature
---------------------------  --------------  ----------------
dirichlet                    alpha           (n)       -> (n)
multinomial                  n, pvals        (),(n)    -> (n)
multivariate_normal          mean, cov       (n),(n,n) -> (n)
multivariate_hypergeometric  colors, nsample (n),()    -> (n)

@bashtage has a pull request to add broadcasting to multinomial. As an example, suppose I have four values of n, say 2, 5, 10 and 20, and I have two discrete probability distributions of length 3, say [0.1, 0.2, 0.7] and [0.8, 0.2, 0.0], and I want to generate 10 multinomial variates for each combination of those inputs. With the code in @bashtage's PR, we can write:

In [85]: n = np.array([2, 5, 10, 20]).reshape(-1, 1)

In [86]: pvals = np.array([[0.1, 0.2, 0.7], [0.8, 0.2, 0.0]])

In [87]: rng = np.random.default_rng()

In [88]: x = rng.multinomial(n, pvals, size=(10, 4, 2))

In [89]: x.shape
Out[89]: (10, 4, 2, 3)

The shape of the output has three sources: (10,) is the number of variates that we wanted for each combination of input parameters; (4, 2) is the broadcast shape of the input parameters, without the dimension associated with the gufunc signature; (3,) is the dimension associated with each variate.

Note that size is not the shape of the output array--size does not include the dimension associated with the variates themselves.

The question is how to adapt this to the other multivariate distribution methods.
rephrased_statement: Considering the example where `n = np.array([2,5,10,20]).reshape(-1,1)` and `pvals` is a (2,3) matrix, does the resulting shape `(10,4,2,3)` imply a generalizable broadcasting contract for all SciPy multivariate RNGs, or are there hidden edge cases that could diverge from NumPy's design?

This issue is motivated by ongoing work in SciPy to improve the existing multivariate distributions and add new ones. We'd like to be sure that, if possible, enhancements that we make remain consistent with the current and future behavior of NumPy's multivariate distributions.

The specific issue is how the size parameter interacts with broadcasting of the distribution parameters, some of which are 1-d or 2-d arrays rather than scalars.

I'm going to refer to gufunc broadcasting, so it will be helpful to have the gufunc signatures of the existing multivariate distributions (even though they are not actually implemented as gufuncs):

Name                         Parameters      Gufunc signature
---------------------------  --------------  ----------------
dirichlet                    alpha           (n)       -> (n)
multinomial                  n, pvals        (),(n)    -> (n)
multivariate_normal          mean, cov       (n),(n,n) -> (n)
multivariate_hypergeometric  colors, nsample (n),()    -> (n)

@bashtage has a pull request to add broadcasting to multinomial. As an example, suppose I have four values of n, say 2, 5, 10 and 20, and I have two discrete probability distributions of length 3, say [0.1, 0.2, 0.7] and [0.8, 0.2, 0.0], and I want to generate 10 multinomial variates for each combination of those inputs. With the code in @bashtage's PR, we can write:

In [85]: n = np.array([2, 5, 10, 20]).reshape(-1, 1)

In [86]: pvals = np.array([[0.1, 0.2, 0.7], [0.8, 0.2, 0.0]])

In [87]: rng = np.random.default_rng()

In [88]: x = rng.multinomial(n, pvals, size=(10, 4, 2))

In [89]: x.shape
Out[89]: (10, 4, 2, 3)

The shape of the output has three sources: (10,) is the number of variates that we wanted for each combination of input parameters; (4, 2) is the broadcast shape of the input parameters, without the dimension associated with the gufunc signature; (3,) is the dimension associated with each variate.

Note that size is not the shape of the output array--size does not include the dimension associated with the variates themselves.

The question is how to adapt this to the other multivariate distribution methods.
rephrased_statement: So, we're trying to upgrade SciPy's multivariate distribution suite while keeping everything in sync with NumPy's own multivariate APIs now and down the road. To make sense of it, I'm looking at the gufunc signatures that describe each distribution – like `multivariate_normal` being `(n),(n,n) -> (n)` – even though they aren't implemented as real gufuncs yet. This issue is motivated by ongoing work in SciPy to improve the existing multivariate distributions and add new ones. We'd like to be sure that, if possible, enhancements that we make remain consistent with the current and future behavior of NumPy's multivariate distributions.

The specific issue is how the size parameter interacts with broadcasting of the distribution parameters, some of which are 1-d or 2-d arrays rather than scalars.

I'm going to refer to gufunc broadcasting, so it will be helpful to have the gufunc signatures of the existing multivariate distributions (even though they are not actually implemented as gufuncs):

Name                         Parameters      Gufunc signature
---------------------------  --------------  ----------------
dirichlet                    alpha           (n)       -> (n)
multinomial                  n, pvals        (),(n)    -> (n)
multivariate_normal          mean, cov       (n),(n,n) -> (n)
multivariate_hypergeometric  colors, nsample (n),()    -> (n)

@bashtage has a pull request to add broadcasting to multinomial. As an example, suppose I have four values of n, say 2, 5, 10 and 20, and I have two discrete probability distributions of length 3, say [0.1, 0.2, 0.7] and [0.8, 0.2, 0.0], and I want to generate 10 multinomial variates for each combination of those inputs. With the code in @bashtage's PR, we can write:

In [85]: n = np.array([2, 5, 10, 20]).reshape(-1, 1)

In [86]: pvals = np.array([[0.1, 0.2, 0.7], [0.8, 0.2, 0.0]])

In [87]: rng = np.random.default_rng()

In [88]: x = rng.multinomial(n, pvals, size=(10, 4, 2))

In [89]: x.shape
Out[89]: (10, 4, 2, 3)

The shape of the output has three sources: (10,) is the number of variates that we wanted for each combination of input parameters; (4, 2) is the broadcast shape of the input parameters, without the dimension associated with the gufunc signature; (3,) is the dimension associated with each variate.

Note that size is not the shape of the output array--size does not include the dimension associated with the variates themselves.

The question is how to adapt this to the other multivariate distribution methods.
rephrased_statement:
We will guarantee that enhancements to SciPy’s multivariate distributions do not break NumPy’s expected behavior by standardizing how `size` works with broadcasted parameters. The gufunc signatures—`dirichlet(alpha) -> (n)`, `multinomial(n, pvals) -> (n)`, `multivariate_normal(mean, cov) -> (n)`, `multivariate_hypergeometric(colors, nsample) -> (n)`—provide a clear template. For instance, the snippet
```python
n = np.arange(2,21,3).reshape(-1,1)
pvals = np.array([[0.1,0.2,0.7],[0.8,0.2,0.0]])
rng = np.random.default_rng()
out = rng.multinomial(n, pvals, size=(10,4,2))
print(out.shape)  # (10,4,2,3)
```
shows that `size` determines the number of samples per broadcasted parameter combination, separate from the variate dimension. This broadcasting logic will be extended to the rest of the multivariate distribution API.

This issue is motivated by ongoing work in SciPy to improve the existing multivariate distributions and add new ones. We'd like to be sure that, if possible, enhancements that we make remain consistent with the current and future behavior of NumPy's multivariate distributions.

The specific issue is how the size parameter interacts with broadcasting of the distribution parameters, some of which are 1-d or 2-d arrays rather than scalars.

I'm going to refer to gufunc broadcasting, so it will be helpful to have the gufunc signatures of the existing multivariate distributions (even though they are not actually implemented as gufuncs):

Name                         Parameters      Gufunc signature
---------------------------  --------------  ----------------
dirichlet                    alpha           (n)       -> (n)
multinomial                  n, pvals        (),(n)    -> (n)
multivariate_normal          mean, cov       (n),(n,n) -> (n)
multivariate_hypergeometric  colors, nsample (n),()    -> (n)

@bashtage has a pull request to add broadcasting to multinomial. As an example, suppose I have four values of n, say 2, 5, 10 and 20, and I have two discrete probability distributions of length 3, say [0.1, 0.2, 0.7] and [0.8, 0.2, 0.0], and I want to generate 10 multinomial variates for each combination of those inputs. With the code in @bashtage's PR, we can write:

In [85]: n = np.array([2, 5, 10, 20]).reshape(-1, 1)

In [86]: pvals = np.array([[0.1, 0.2, 0.7], [0.8, 0.2, 0.0]])

In [87]: rng = np.random.default_rng()

In [88]: x = rng.multinomial(n, pvals, size=(10, 4, 2))

In [89]: x.shape
Out[89]: (10, 4, 2, 3)

The shape of the output has three sources: (10,) is the number of variates that we wanted for each combination of input parameters; (4, 2) is the broadcast shape of the input parameters, without the dimension associated with the gufunc signature; (3,) is the dimension associated with each variate.

Note that size is not the shape of the output array--size does not include the dimension associated with the variates themselves.

The question is how to adapt this to the other multivariate distribution methods.
rephrased_statement: I'm not really sure how the `size` parameter is supposed to work together with broadcasting for the other multivariate distribution functions—does it include the broadcasted dimensions of the parameters, or is it just the number of variates we ask for? Any clarification would be great.

This issue is motivated by ongoing work in SciPy to improve the existing multivariate distributions and add new ones. We'd like to be sure that, if possible, enhancements that we make remain consistent with the current and future behavior of NumPy's multivariate distributions.

The specific issue is how the size parameter interacts with broadcasting of the distribution parameters, some of which are 1-d or 2-d arrays rather than scalars.

I'm going to refer to gufunc broadcasting, so it will be helpful to have the gufunc signatures of the existing multivariate distributions (even though they are not actually implemented as gufuncs):

Name                         Parameters      Gufunc signature
---------------------------  --------------  ----------------
dirichlet                    alpha           (n)       -> (n)
multinomial                  n, pvals        (),(n)    -> (n)
multivariate_normal          mean, cov       (n),(n,n) -> (n)
multivariate_hypergeometric  colors, nsample (n),()    -> (n)

@bashtage has a pull request to add broadcasting to multinomial. As an example, suppose I have four values of n, say 2, 5, 10 and 20, and I have two discrete probability distributions of length 3, say [0.1, 0.2, 0.7] and [0.8, 0.2, 0.0], and I want to generate 10 multinomial variates for each combination of those inputs. With the code in @bashtage's PR, we can write:

In [85]: n = np.array([2, 5, 10, 20]).reshape(-1, 1)

In [86]: pvals = np.array([[0.1, 0.2, 0.7], [0.8, 0.2, 0.0]])

In [87]: rng = np.random.default_rng()

In [88]: x = rng.multinomial(n, pvals, size=(10, 4, 2))

In [89]: x.shape
Out[89]: (10, 4, 2, 3)

The shape of the output has three sources: (10,) is the number of variates that we wanted for each combination of input parameters; (4, 2) is the broadcast shape of the input parameters, without the dimension associated with the gufunc signature; (3,) is the dimension associated with each variate.

Note that size is not the shape of the output array--size does not include the dimension associated with the variates themselves.

The question is how to adapt this to the other multivariate distribution methods.
rephrased_statement: Could someone explain how the `size` keyword should be interpreted for broadcasting across multivariate distribution parameters that are not simple scalars? In the multinomial example, `size` governs the number of generated variates but does not account for the trailing dimension that represents each variate's outcome. I'm not sure how to extend this logic to distributions like `dirichlet(alpha)` or `multivariate_hypergeometric(colors, nsample)`.

This issue is motivated by ongoing work in SciPy to improve the existing multivariate distributions and add new ones. We'd like to be sure that, if possible, enhancements that we make remain consistent with the current and future behavior of NumPy's multivariate distributions.

The specific issue is how the size parameter interacts with broadcasting of the distribution parameters, some of which are 1-d or 2-d arrays rather than scalars.

I'm going to refer to gufunc broadcasting, so it will be helpful to have the gufunc signatures of the existing multivariate distributions (even though they are not actually implemented as gufuncs):

Name                         Parameters      Gufunc signature
---------------------------  --------------  ----------------
dirichlet                    alpha           (n)       -> (n)
multinomial                  n, pvals        (),(n)    -> (n)
multivariate_normal          mean, cov       (n),(n,n) -> (n)
multivariate_hypergeometric  colors, nsample (n),()    -> (n)

@bashtage has a pull request to add broadcasting to multinomial. As an example, suppose I have four values of n, say 2, 5, 10 and 20, and I have two discrete probability distributions of length 3, say [0.1, 0.2, 0.7] and [0.8, 0.2, 0.0], and I want to generate 10 multinomial variates for each combination of those inputs. With the code in @bashtage's PR, we can write:

In [85]: n = np.array([2, 5, 10, 20]).reshape(-1, 1)

In [86]: pvals = np.array([[0.1, 0.2, 0.7], [0.8, 0.2, 0.0]])

In [87]: rng = np.random.default_rng()

In [88]: x = rng.multinomial(n, pvals, size=(10, 4, 2))

In [89]: x.shape
Out[89]: (10, 4, 2, 3)

The shape of the output has three sources: (10,) is the number of variates that we wanted for each combination of input parameters; (4, 2) is the broadcast shape of the input parameters, without the dimension associated with the gufunc signature; (3,) is the dimension associated with each variate.

Note that size is not the shape of the output array--size does not include the dimension associated with the variates themselves.

The question is how to adapt this to the other multivariate distribution methods.
rephrased_statement: We're aiming to align SciPy's upcoming multivariate distribution enhancements with NumPy's existing (and future) broadcasting semantics; however, I'm uncertain how the `size` argument should co‑operate with gufunc‑style broadcasting when the distribution parameters are 1‑D or 2‑D arrays rather than scalars.

original_statement:
This issue is motivated by ongoing work in SciPy to improve the existing multivariate distributions and add new ones. We'd like to be sure that, if possible, enhancements that we make remain consistent with the current and future behavior of NumPy's multivariate distributions.

The specific issue is how the size parameter interacts with broadcasting of the distribution parameters, some of which are 1-d or 2-d arrays rather than scalars.

I'm going to refer to gufunc broadcasting, so it will be helpful to have the gufunc signatures of the existing multivariate distributions (even though they are not actually implemented as gufuncs):

Name                         Parameters      Gufunc signature
---------------------------  --------------  ----------------
dirichlet                    alpha           (n)       -> (n)
multinomial                  n, pvals        (),(n)    -> (n)
multivariate_normal          mean, cov       (n),(n,n) -> (n)
multivariate_hypergeometric  colors, nsample (n),()    -> (n)

@bashtage has a pull request to add broadcasting to multinomial. As an example, suppose I have four values of n, say 2, 5, 10 and 20, and I have two discrete probability distributions of length 3, say [0.1, 0.2, 0.7] and [0.8, 0.2, 0.0], and I want to generate 10 multinomial variates for each combination of those inputs. With the code in @bashtage's PR, we can write:

In [85]: n = np.array([2, 5, 10, 20]).reshape(-1, 1)

In [86]: pvals = np.array([[0.1, 0.2, 0.7], [0.8, 0.2, 0.0]])

In [87]: rng = np.random.default_rng()

In [88]: x = rng.multinomial(n, pvals, size=(10, 4, 2))

In [89]: x.shape
Out[89]: (10, 4, 2, 3)

The shape of the output has three sources: (10,) is the number of variates that we wanted for each combination of input parameters; (4, 2) is the broadcast shape of the input parameters, without the dimension associated with the gufunc signature; (3,) is the dimension associated with each variate.

Note that size is not the shape of the output array--size does not include the dimension associated with the variates themselves.

The question is how to adapt this to the other multivariate distribution methods.
rephrased_statement: Hey team, I'm digging into the SciPy work on polishing up the existing multivariate distributions and adding a few new ones. The big question for us is making sure any tweaks we roll out stay compatible with both the current NumPy multivariate behavior and any future changes they might make. The part that's giving me a headache is the `size` argument – it seems to clash with how the distribution parameters get broadcasted, especially when those parameters are 1‑D or 2‑D arrays instead of simple scalars. I'm using the gufunc‑style signatures as a reference (even though they aren’t real gufuncs yet) to see how things should line up. For example, with a Dirichlet you have `(n) -> (n)`, multinomial uses `(),(n) -> (n)`, and so on. The goal is to figure out a clean way to extend the broadcasting logic that @bashtage added for `multinomial` to the other multivariate distribution functions.

This issue is motivated by ongoing work in SciPy to improve the existing multivariate distributions and add new ones. We'd like to be sure that, if possible, enhancements that we make remain consistent with the current and future behavior of NumPy's multivariate distributions.

The specific issue is how the size parameter interacts with broadcasting of the distribution parameters, some of which are 1-d or 2-d arrays rather than scalars.

I'm going to refer to gufunc broadcasting, so it will be helpful to have the gufunc signatures of the existing multivariate distributions (even though they are not actually implemented as gufuncs):

Name                         Parameters      Gufunc signature
---------------------------  --------------  ----------------
dirichlet                    alpha           (n)       -> (n)
multinomial                  n, pvals        (),(n)    -> (n)
multivariate_normal          mean, cov       (n),(n,n) -> (n)
multivariate_hypergeometric  colors, nsample (n),()    -> (n)

@bashtage has a pull request to add broadcasting to multinomial. As an example, suppose I have four values of n, say 2, 5, 10 and 20, and I have two discrete probability distributions of length 3, say [0.1, 0.2, 0.7] and [0.8, 0.2, 0.0], and I want to generate 10 multinomial variates for each combination of those inputs. With the code in @bashtage's PR, we can write:

In [85]: n = np.array([2, 5, 10, 20]).reshape(-1, 1)

In [86]: pvals = np.array([[0.1, 0.2, 0.7], [0.8, 0.2, 0.0]])

In [87]: rng = np.random.default_rng()

In [88]: x = rng.multinomial(n, pvals, size=(10, 4, 2))

In [89]: x.shape
Out[89]: (10, 4, 2, 3)

The shape of the output has three sources: (10,) is the number of variates that we wanted for each combination of input parameters; (4, 2) is the broadcast shape of the input parameters, without the dimension associated with the gufunc signature; (3,) is the dimension associated with each variate.

Note that size is not the shape of the output array--size does not include the dimension associated with the variates themselves.

The question is how to adapt this to the other multivariate distribution methods.
rephrased_statement: As part of the effort to upgrade SciPy's multivariate distribution capabilities, we are seeking assurance that any modifications will not diverge from the semantics established by NumPy's multivariate distribution functions. The specific unknown concerns the relationship between the `size` argument and the broadcasting of parameter arrays—such as the `pvals` matrix for multinomial or the covariance matrix for multivariate normal—especially when those parameters are not scalars. Clarification on how to formulate the gufunc signatures and expected output shapes for these scenarios would be highly valuable.

I accidentally discovered that nn.Linear with datatype float16/bfloat16 can produce significant numerical errors on sliced tensors:
 import torch
 torch.random.manual_seed(42)
 from torch import nn
 

 dtype = torch.float16
 batch, seq, embed_dim, delay = 2, 16, 4, 2
 x1 = torch.randn(batch, seq, embed_dim, device="cuda", dtype=dtype)
 x2 = x1[:, delay:]
 assert torch.allclose(x1[:, delay:], x2)
 net = nn.Linear(embed_dim, embed_dim).to("cuda").to(dtype=dtype)
 out1 = net(x1)
 out2 = net(x2)
 print((out1[:, delay:] - out2).abs().max())
 assert torch.allclose(out1[:, delay:], out2)
 

 I got the output like this:
 tensor(0.0010, device='cuda:0', dtype=torch.float16, grad_fn=<MaxBackward1>)
 Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "/home/jewel/Workspaces/cusrl/test.py", line 14, in <module>
  assert torch.allclose(out1[:, delay:], out2)
 AssertionError
 

 If the type is bfloat16, the error is even greater:
 tensor(0.0078, device='cuda:0', dtype=torch.bfloat16, grad_fn=<MaxBackward1>)
 Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "/home/jewel/Workspaces/cusrl/test.py", line 14, in <module>
  assert torch.allclose(out1[:, delay:], out2)
 AssertionError
 

 However, if the tensor is cloned after sliced x2 = x1[:, delay:].clone() or the type is float32, it will produce an error of exactly zero.
 tensor(0., device='cuda:0', grad_fn=<MaxBackward1>)
 

 I don't know if this is an allowable margin of error or a bug.
rephrased_statement: In an ad‑hoc validation of half‑precision arithmetic on CUDA I discovered that `nn.Linear` can emit divergent results when its input is a non‑contiguous view of a `float16` (or `bfloat16`) tensor.  The reproducible example seeds the random generator, creates `x1 = torch.randn(2,16,4, device="cuda", dtype=torch.float16)`, then extracts `x2 = x1[:, 2:]`.  A preliminary `torch.allclose` confirms the slices are numerically identical.  After casting a linear module to the same dtype (`net = nn.Linear(4,4).to("cuda").to(dtype=torch.float16)`), the forward passes yield `out1 = net(x1)` and `out2 = net(x2)`.  The diagnostic `print((out1[:, 2:] - out2).abs().max())` prints `tensor(0.0010, ...)`, and the following `assert torch.allclose` raises an error.  The phenomenon is exacerbated in `bfloat16` (`0.0078`).  A simple `clone()` on the slice or upgrading to `float32` restores exact equality.  I'm left wondering whether this behavior falls under the permissible error margin for half‑precision GEMM on strided tensors, or whether it reveals a latent bug in the ATen kernel implementations.

```python
class Kls: pass

a = Kls()
a.mean = None
np.mean(a)  # → TypeError: 'NoneType' object is not callable

a.mean = lambda: 0
np.mean(a)  # → TypeError: <lambda>() got an unexpected keyword argument 'axis'
```
What’s happening is that `np.mean` checks for a `mean` attribute on the incoming object and then calls it assuming it follows NumPy’s exact signature. This was a total surprise to me; I had no clue NumPy would be so presumptuous about external `mean` methods.

This issue is motivated by ongoing work in SciPy to improve the existing multivariate distributions and add new ones. We'd like to be sure that, if possible, enhancements that we make remain consistent with the current and future behavior of NumPy's multivariate distributions.

The specific issue is how the size parameter interacts with broadcasting of the distribution parameters, some of which are 1-d or 2-d arrays rather than scalars.

I'm going to refer to gufunc broadcasting, so it will be helpful to have the gufunc signatures of the existing multivariate distributions (even though they are not actually implemented as gufuncs):

Name                         Parameters      Gufunc signature
---------------------------  --------------  ----------------
dirichlet                    alpha           (n)       -> (n)
multinomial                  n, pvals        (),(n)    -> (n)
multivariate_normal          mean, cov       (n),(n,n) -> (n)
multivariate_hypergeometric  colors, nsample (n),()    -> (n)

@bashtage has a pull request to add broadcasting to multinomial. As an example, suppose I have four values of n, say 2, 5, 10 and 20, and I have two discrete probability distributions of length 3, say [0.1, 0.2, 0.7] and [0.8, 0.2, 0.0], and I want to generate 10 multinomial variates for each combination of those inputs. With the code in @bashtage's PR, we can write:

In [85]: n = np.array([2, 5, 10, 20]).reshape(-1, 1)

In [86]: pvals = np.array([[0.1, 0.2, 0.7], [0.8, 0.2, 0.0]])

In [87]: rng = np.random.default_rng()

In [88]: x = rng.multinomial(n, pvals, size=(10, 4, 2))

In [89]: x.shape
Out[89]: (10, 4, 2, 3)

The shape of the output has three sources: (10,) is the number of variates that we wanted for each combination of input parameters; (4, 2) is the broadcast shape of the input parameters, without the dimension associated with the gufunc signature; (3,) is the dimension associated with each variate.

Note that size is not the shape of the output array--size does not include the dimension associated with the variates themselves.

The question is how to adapt this to the other multivariate distribution methods.

original_statement:
This issue is motivated by ongoing work in SciPy to improve the existing multivariate distributions and add new ones. We'd like to be sure that, if possible, enhancements that we make remain consistent with the current and future behavior of NumPy's multivariate distributions.

The specific issue is how the size parameter interacts with broadcasting of the distribution parameters, some of which are 1-d or 2-d arrays rather than scalars.

I'm going to refer to gufunc broadcasting, so it will be helpful to have the gufunc signatures of the existing multivariate distributions (even though they are not actually implemented as gufuncs):

Name                         Parameters      Gufunc signature
---------------------------  --------------  ----------------
dirichlet                    alpha           (n)       -> (n)
multinomial                  n, pvals        (),(n)    -> (n)
multivariate_normal          mean, cov       (n),(n,n) -> (n)
multivariate_hypergeometric  colors, nsample (n),()    -> (n)

@bashtage has a pull request to add broadcasting to multinomial. As an example, suppose I have four values of n, say 2, 5, 10 and 20, and I have two discrete probability distributions of length 3, say [0.1, 0.2, 0.7] and [0.8, 0.2, 0.0], and I want to generate 10 multinomial variates for each combination of those inputs. With the code in @bashtage's PR, we can write:

In [85]: n = np.array([2, 5, 10, 20]).reshape(-1, 1)

In [86]: pvals = np.array([[0.1, 0.2, 0.7], [0.8, 0.2, 0.0]])

In [87]: rng = np.random.default_rng()

In [88]: x = rng.multinomial(n, pvals, size=(10, 4, 2))

In [89]: x.shape
Out[89]: (10, 4, 2, 3)

The shape of the output has three sources: (10,) is the number of variates that we wanted for each combination of input parameters; (4, 2) is the broadcast shape of the input parameters, without the dimension associated with the gufunc signature; (3,) is the dimension associated with each variate.

Note that size is not the shape of the output array--size does not include the dimension associated with the variates themselves.

The question is how to adapt this to the other multivariate distribution methods.
rephrased_statement: To keep SciPy’s multivariate distribution suite compatible with NumPy’s semantics, we will adopt a broadcasting strategy that respects the `size` parameter and the gufunc‑style signatures of each distribution. The signatures—`dirichlet(alpha) -> (n)`, `multinomial(n, pvals) -> (n)`, `multivariate_normal(mean, cov) -> (n)`, `multivariate_hypergeometric(colors, nsample) -> (n)`—guide how parameter arrays of different dimensions are combined. In practice, using `rng.multinomial` with `n = np.array([2,5,10,20]).reshape(-1,1)`, `pvals = np.array([[0.1,0.2,0.7],[0.8,0.2,0.0]])`, and `size=(10,4,2)` yields a shape `(10,4,2,3)`. This demonstrates that `size` controls the number of draws per broadcasted parameter set, while the trailing dimension reflects the outcome size. We will replicate this approach for `multivariate_normal`, `dirichlet`, and other distributions.

Since there is a well defined interoperability protocol I was assuming that it is safe to call numpy functions on foreign objects, until I discovered this strange behaviour:

>>> import numpy as np
>>> class Kls: pass
...
>>> a = Kls()
>>> a.mean = None
>>> np.mean(a)
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "<stdin>", line 1, in <module>
  File "/Users/miccoli/work/uvenv/bigdata/.venv/lib/python3.12/site-packages/numpy/_core/fromnumeric.py", line 3858, in mean
    return mean(axis=axis, dtype=dtype, out=out, **kwargs)
           ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
TypeError: 'NoneType' object is not callable
>>> a.mean = lambda : 0
>>> np.mean(a)
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "<stdin>", line 1, in <module>
  File "/Users/miccoli/work/uvenv/bigdata/.venv/lib/python3.12/site-packages/numpy/_core/fromnumeric.py", line 3858, in mean
    return mean(axis=axis, dtype=dtype, out=out, **kwargs)
           ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
TypeError: <lambda>() got an unexpected keyword argument 'axis'

So if np.mean(a) discovers that a has a mean attribute, it blindly assumes that it is a method with the same semantics and signature of np.mean.

This is crazy! numpy does not owns the mean method and in fact other libraries implemented it in different ways:

>>> import polars as pl
>>> a = pl.Series([0, 1, 2])
>>> np.mean(a) #broken
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "<stdin>", line 1, in <module>
  File "/Users/miccoli/work/uvenv/bigdata/.venv/lib/python3.12/site-packages/numpy/_core/fromnumeric.py", line 3858, in mean
    return mean(axis=axis, dtype=dtype, out=out, **kwargs)
           ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
TypeError: Series.mean() got an unexpected keyword argument 'axis'
>>> np.mean(np.asarray(a)) #works
np.float64(1.0)
rephrased_statement: I assumed NumPy's protocol covered all cases, but if an object defines its own `mean` (even as `None`), `np.mean` will try to use it and pass its own keyword arguments, leading to errors like `'NoneType' object is not callable` or `got an unexpected keyword argument 'axis'`.

Since there is a well defined interoperability protocol I was assuming that it is safe to call numpy functions on foreign objects, until I discovered this strange behaviour:

>>> import numpy as np
>>> class Kls: pass
...
>>> a = Kls()
>>> a.mean = None
>>> np.mean(a)
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "<stdin>", line 1, in <module>
  File "/Users/miccoli/work/uvenv/bigdata/.venv/lib/python3.12/site-packages/numpy/_core/fromnumeric.py", line 3858, in mean
    return mean(axis=axis, dtype=dtype, out=out, **kwargs)
           ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
TypeError: 'NoneType' object is not callable
>>> a.mean = lambda : 0
>>> np.mean(a)
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "<stdin>", line 1, in <module>
  File "/Users/miccoli/work/uvenv/bigdata/.venv/lib/python3.12/site-packages/numpy/_core/fromnumeric.py", line 3858, in mean
    return mean(axis=axis, dtype=dtype, out=out, **kwargs)
           ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
TypeError: <lambda>() got an unexpected keyword argument 'axis'

So if np.mean(a) discovers that a has a mean attribute, it blindly assumes that it is a method with the same semantics and signature of np.mean.

This is crazy! numpy does not owns the mean method and in fact other libraries implemented it in different ways:

>>> import polars as pl
>>> a = pl.Series([0, 1, 2])
>>> np.mean(a) #broken
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "<stdin>", line 1, in <module>
  File "/Users/miccoli/work/uvenv/bigdata/.venv/lib/python3.12/site-packages/numpy/_core/fromnumeric.py", line 3858, in mean
    return mean(axis=axis, dtype=dtype, out=out, **kwargs)
           ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
TypeError: Series.mean() got an unexpected keyword argument 'axis'
>>> np.mean(np.asarray(a)) #works
np.float64(1.0)
rephrased_statement: Turns out my assumption that np.mean would safely handle foreign objects was wrong; if the object has a `mean` attribute, numpy calls it with its own kwargs, which blows up if the signature doesn't match.

This issue is motivated by ongoing work in SciPy to improve the existing multivariate distributions and add new ones. We'd like to be sure that, if possible, enhancements that we make remain consistent with the current and future behavior of NumPy's multivariate distributions.

The specific issue is how the size parameter interacts with broadcasting of the distribution parameters, some of which are 1-d or 2-d arrays rather than scalars.

I'm going to refer to gufunc broadcasting, so it will be helpful to have the gufunc signatures of the existing multivariate distributions (even though they are not actually implemented as gufuncs):

Name                         Parameters      Gufunc signature
---------------------------  --------------  ----------------
dirichlet                    alpha           (n)       -> (n)
multinomial                  n, pvals        (),(n)    -> (n)
multivariate_normal          mean, cov       (n),(n,n) -> (n)
multivariate_hypergeometric  colors, nsample (n),()    -> (n)

@bashtage has a pull request to add broadcasting to multinomial. As an example, suppose I have four values of n, say 2, 5, 10 and 20, and I have two discrete probability distributions of length 3, say [0.1, 0.2, 0.7] and [0.8, 0.2, 0.0], and I want to generate 10 multinomial variates for each combination of those inputs. With the code in @bashtage's PR, we can write:

In [85]: n = np.array([2, 5, 10, 20]).reshape(-1, 1)

In [86]: pvals = np.array([[0.1, 0.2, 0.7], [0.8, 0.2, 0.0]])

In [87]: rng = np.random.default_rng()

In [88]: x = rng.multinomial(n, pvals, size=(10, 4, 2))

In [89]: x.shape
Out[89]: (10, 4, 2, 3)

The shape of the output has three sources: (10,) is the number of variates that we wanted for each combination of input parameters; (4, 2) is the broadcast shape of the input parameters, without the dimension associated with the gufunc signature; (3,) is the dimension associated with each variate.

Note that size is not the shape of the output array--size does not include the dimension associated with the variates themselves.

The question is how to adapt this to the other multivariate distribution methods.
rephrased_statement: Quick update on the SciPy multivariate distribution revamp: we want any new features or fixes to stay compatible with NumPy's existing and future multivariate distribution behavior. The main puzzle is how the `size` keyword works together with broadcasting when the distribution's parameters are supplied as arrays (some 1‑D, some 2‑D) rather than plain scalars. I'm mapping out the gufunc signatures for each distribution – for instance, `dirichlet` uses `(n) -> (n)` and `multinomial` uses `(),(n) -> (n)` – to see how the broadcasting should behave. @bashtage's PR gives us a nice example for `multinomial`, where you can pass a vector of `n` values and a matrix of `pvals` and get a nicely shaped output. Now we need to figure out how to apply that same broadcasting logic to the other multivariate methods so that `size` only controls the number of draws and not the internal variate dimensions.

Since there is a well defined interoperability protocol I was assuming that it is safe to call numpy functions on foreign objects, until I discovered this strange behaviour:

>>> import numpy as np
>>> class Kls: pass
...
>>> a = Kls()
>>> a.mean = None
>>> np.mean(a)
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "<stdin>", line 1, in <module>
  File "/Users/miccoli/work/uvenv/bigdata/.venv/lib/python3.12/site-packages/numpy/_core/fromnumeric.py", line 3858, in mean
    return mean(axis=axis, dtype=dtype, out=out, **kwargs)
           ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
TypeError: 'NoneType' object is not callable
>>> a.mean = lambda : 0
>>> np.mean(a)
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "<stdin>", line 1, in <module>
  File "/Users/miccoli/work/uvenv/bigdata/.venv/lib/python3.12/site-packages/numpy/_core/fromnumeric.py", line 3858, in mean
    return mean(axis=axis, dtype=dtype, out=out, **kwargs)
           ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
TypeError: <lambda>() got an unexpected keyword argument 'axis'

So if np.mean(a) discovers that a has a mean attribute, it blindly assumes that it is a method with the same semantics and signature of np.mean.

This is crazy! numpy does not owns the mean method and in fact other libraries implemented it in different ways:

>>> import polars as pl
>>> a = pl.Series([0, 1, 2])
>>> np.mean(a) #broken
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "<stdin>", line 1, in <module>
  File "/Users/miccoli/work/uvenv/bigdata/.venv/lib/python3.12/site-packages/numpy/_core/fromnumeric.py", line 3858, in mean
    return mean(axis=axis, dtype=dtype, out=out, **kwargs)
           ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
TypeError: Series.mean() got an unexpected keyword argument 'axis'
>>> np.mean(np.asarray(a)) #works
np.float64(1.0)
rephrased_statement: I was operating under the belief that the well‑defined interoperability protocol would let me invoke NumPy functions on arbitrary objects without issue. However, after assigning `a.mean = None` and later a lambda to a simple class instance, `np.mean(a)` raised a TypeError because NumPy blindly forwards its `axis`, `dtype`, and other arguments to whatever `mean` attribute it finds, without checking compatibility. This also broke when I tried a Polars Series – NumPy tried to call `Series.mean(axis=…)` and failed, even though converting to a NumPy array works fine.

Using MPS for BERT inference appears to produce about a 2x slowdown compared to the CPU. Here is code to reproduce the issue:
 # MPS Version
 from transformers import AutoTokenizer, BertForSequenceClassification
 import timeit
 import torch
 

 tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained("bert-base-cased")
 model = BertForSequenceClassification.from_pretrained("bert-base-cased").to(torch.device("mps"))
 

 tokens = tokenizer.tokenize("Hello world, this is michael!")
 tids = tokenizer.convert_tokens_to_ids(tokens)
 with torch.no_grad():
  t_tids = torch.tensor([tids]*64, device=torch.device("mps"))
  res = timeit.timeit(lambda: model(input_ids=t_tids), number=100)
 print(res)
 

 torch.backends.mps.is_available() reports True as expected.
 I chose a batch size of 64, since that was mentioned on the blog post for the ~5x speedup in Huggingface BERT.
 Running this benchmark, swapping "mps" and "cpu" for the devices, I get:
 CPU 18.38 s
 MPS 36.00 s
 And, for comparison, running this same snippet on an A10G using CUDA 11.6 on an AWS g5.xlarge instance (ubuntu 20.04, pytorch 1.11.0 compiled from source), I get:
 CUDA 0.82 s
 I used the no_grad() construction due to the comment mentioned on #77753.
 I used today's nightly build. Furthermore, I also built PyTorch from source and observed no differences on the results here. Lastly, I confirmed with Activity Monitor and powermetrics that the GPU is in fact being used, seeing GPU usage at 98.8%, GPU power spike to 15711 mW when running the MPS benchmark, and CPU power spiking as expected when running the CPU benchmark.
 So it does seem like things are "hooked up" right, just not efficient.
 As a side note, when building PyTorch from source, I observed in the CMake logs that Accelerate.framework was selected as the BLAS library, but sadly I didn't observe any power consumption by the ANE module, which is too bad.
rephrased_statement: Running the following benchmark shows that BERT inference on an MPS backend is about twice as slow as on the CPU (36 s vs 18 s for batch‑size 64), whereas the same model on CUDA finishes in ~0.8 s. All indicators (torch.backends.mps.is_available(), GPU usage, power spikes) suggest the GPU is active. I'm unsure whether this 2× slowdown is due to a misconfiguration, a missing optimization in PyTorch's MPS support, or simply the current state of MPS performance.

Since there is a well defined interoperability protocol I was assuming that it is safe to call numpy functions on foreign objects, until I discovered this strange behaviour:

>>> import numpy as np
>>> class Kls: pass
...
>>> a = Kls()
>>> a.mean = None
>>> np.mean(a)
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "<stdin>", line 1, in <module>
  File "/Users/miccoli/work/uvenv/bigdata/.venv/lib/python3.12/site-packages/numpy/_core/fromnumeric.py", line 3858, in mean
    return mean(axis=axis, dtype=dtype, out=out, **kwargs)
           ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
TypeError: 'NoneType' object is not callable
>>> a.mean = lambda : 0
>>> np.mean(a)
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "<stdin>", line 1, in <module>
  File "/Users/miccoli/work/uvenv/bigdata/.venv/lib/python3.12/site-packages/numpy/_core/fromnumeric.py", line 3858, in mean
    return mean(axis=axis, dtype=dtype, out=out, **kwargs)
           ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
TypeError: <lambda>() got an unexpected keyword argument 'axis'

So if np.mean(a) discovers that a has a mean attribute, it blindly assumes that it is a method with the same semantics and signature of np.mean.

This is crazy! numpy does not owns the mean method and in fact other libraries implemented it in different ways:

>>> import polars as pl
>>> a = pl.Series([0, 1, 2])
>>> np.mean(a) #broken
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "<stdin>", line 1, in <module>
  File "/Users/miccoli/work/uvenv/bigdata/.venv/lib/python3.12/site-packages/numpy/_core/fromnumeric.py", line 3858, in mean
    return mean(axis=axis, dtype=dtype, out=out, **kwargs)
           ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
TypeError: Series.mean() got an unexpected keyword argument 'axis'
>>> np.mean(np.asarray(a)) #works
np.float64(1.0)
rephrased_statement: Wow, I had no idea that NumPy would just call an object's `mean` attribute as if it were its own function. Setting `a.mean = None` or a lambda makes `np.mean(a)` explode with a TypeError about unexpected arguments.

Using MPS for BERT inference appears to produce about a 2x slowdown compared to the CPU. Here is code to reproduce the issue:
 # MPS Version
 from transformers import AutoTokenizer, BertForSequenceClassification
 import timeit
 import torch
 

 tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained("bert-base-cased")
 model = BertForSequenceClassification.from_pretrained("bert-base-cased").to(torch.device("mps"))
 

 tokens = tokenizer.tokenize("Hello world, this is michael!")
 tids = tokenizer.convert_tokens_to_ids(tokens)
 with torch.no_grad():
  t_tids = torch.tensor([tids]*64, device=torch.device("mps"))
  res = timeit.timeit(lambda: model(input_ids=t_tids), number=100)
 print(res)
 

 torch.backends.mps.is_available() reports True as expected.
 I chose a batch size of 64, since that was mentioned on the blog post for the ~5x speedup in Huggingface BERT.
 Running this benchmark, swapping "mps" and "cpu" for the devices, I get:
 CPU 18.38 s
 MPS 36.00 s
 And, for comparison, running this same snippet on an A10G using CUDA 11.6 on an AWS g5.xlarge instance (ubuntu 20.04, pytorch 1.11.0 compiled from source), I get:
 CUDA 0.82 s
 I used the no_grad() construction due to the comment mentioned on #77753.
 I used today's nightly build. Furthermore, I also built PyTorch from source and observed no differences on the results here. Lastly, I confirmed with Activity Monitor and powermetrics that the GPU is in fact being used, seeing GPU usage at 98.8%, GPU power spike to 15711 mW when running the MPS benchmark, and CPU power spiking as expected when running the CPU benchmark.
 So it does seem like things are "hooked up" right, just not efficient.
 As a side note, when building PyTorch from source, I observed in the CMake logs that Accelerate.framework was selected as the BLAS library, but sadly I didn't observe any power consumption by the ANE module, which is too bad.
rephrased_statement: Why does the MPS backend make BERT inference slower than the CPU in my test? I copied the HuggingFace example, set batch size to 64, and measured 36 s on MPS versus 18 s on CPU (and 0.8 s on CUDA). Maybe the BLAS choice or the lack of ANE acceleration is to blame?

This issue is motivated by ongoing work in SciPy to improve the existing multivariate distributions and add new ones. We'd like to be sure that, if possible, enhancements that we make remain consistent with the current and future behavior of NumPy's multivariate distributions.

The specific issue is how the size parameter interacts with broadcasting of the distribution parameters, some of which are 1-d or 2-d arrays rather than scalars.

I'm going to refer to gufunc broadcasting, so it will be helpful to have the gufunc signatures of the existing multivariate distributions (even though they are not actually implemented as gufuncs):

Name                         Parameters      Gufunc signature
---------------------------  --------------  ----------------
dirichlet                    alpha           (n)       -> (n)
multinomial                  n, pvals        (),(n)    -> (n)
multivariate_normal          mean, cov       (n),(n,n) -> (n)
multivariate_hypergeometric  colors, nsample (n),()    -> (n)

@bashtage has a pull request to add broadcasting to multinomial. As an example, suppose I have four values of n, say 2, 5, 10 and 20, and I have two discrete probability distributions of length 3, say [0.1, 0.2, 0.7] and [0.8, 0.2, 0.0], and I want to generate 10 multinomial variates for each combination of those inputs. With the code in @bashtage's PR, we can write:

In [85]: n = np.array([2, 5, 10, 20]).reshape(-1, 1)

In [86]: pvals = np.array([[0.1, 0.2, 0.7], [0.8, 0.2, 0.0]])

In [87]: rng = np.random.default_rng()

In [88]: x = rng.multinomial(n, pvals, size=(10, 4, 2))

In [89]: x.shape
Out[89]: (10, 4, 2, 3)

The shape of the output has three sources: (10,) is the number of variates that we wanted for each combination of input parameters; (4, 2) is the broadcast shape of the input parameters, without the dimension associated with the gufunc signature; (3,) is the dimension associated with each variate.

Note that size is not the shape of the output array--size does not include the dimension associated with the variates themselves.

The question is how to adapt this to the other multivariate distribution methods.
rephrased_statement: Could it be that `size` specifies the count of draws for each broadcasted set of parameters, while the shape implied by the gufunc signature remains independent? If so, how should we reconcile this interpretation across dirichlet, multinomial, multivariate_normal, and multivariate_hypergeometric implementations?
